Future studies should distinguish AcAc from BHB biology, measure nocturnal ketone dynamics, incorporate PSG/EEG spectral endpoints, and separate ketosis-specific effects from weight loss, energy deficit, exercise load, respiratory physiology, circadian timing, and disease-related confounders.

papers.title: Precision Nutrition and Health Outcomes Across the Lifespan.
papers.abstract: Precision nutrition is an emerging paradigm that seeks to tailor dietary recommendations and interventions based on individual and population characteristics. Although advances in multi-omics, wearable sensors, and artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) have accelerated discovery, translation into practice remains limited by fragmented evidence across life stages and insufficient integration of knowledge regarding systems biology and other influences on health. Nutritional needs, vulnerabilities, intervention opportunities, and response heterogeneity evolve dynamically from preconception and pregnancy through infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and older age. These life stage-specific processes intersect with (epi)genetic, metabolic and microbiome factors, as well as social, psychological, behavioral, and environmental/geographic influences, contributing to heterogeneity in health outcomes. Addressing this complexity requires not only multimodal predictive models but also frameworks that integrate data standards and harmonization, systems biology, implementation science, and community engagement. To provide a structured approach to this complexity, we developed a seven-pillar Precision Nutrition Framework encompassing prevention for all, data sources, quantitative sciences, qualitative sciences, intervention implementation, communities, and education and workforce training. Using this framework and a lifespan perspective, we examine opportunities for promoting cardiovascular, pulmonary, hematologic, and circadian/sleep health, synthesize evidence on key nutrients, dietary patterns, and emerging biomarkers, and adapt and expand the "precision nutrition plate" for implementation research in clinical and community settings. We highlight critical research gaps, including the need for phenotype-guided trials, standardized data integration, and scalable implementation strategies. By integrating biological, behavioral, and broader environmental dimensions across the life course, precision nutrition can advance more effective, accessible, and sustainable approaches for disease prevention and health promotion.

papers.title: Emotional Eating Beyond Obesity: A Transdiagnostic Conceptual Analysis of Phenotyping, Measurement, and Priorities for Clinical Validation.
papers.abstract: Background: The concept of emotional eating (EE) originates in the early psychosomatic accounts of overeating, but its nosological status remains contested more than four decades after it was first scientifically explored. Although neither the DSM-5-TR nor the ICD-11 recognizes EE as a discrete entity, clinically significant presentations of EE are described in the literature and can currently be captured under residual diagnostic categories in the absence of specific criteria. Objective: To examine whether EE is best conceptualized as an independent disorder or a dimensional, transdiagnostic, nutritional-behavioral phenotype, and to identify requirements for its clinical validation. Methods: A conceptual analysis supported by a critical synthesis of the literature focused on phenotypic heterogeneity, nutritional correlates, measurement approaches, diagnostic boundaries, and clinical implications of EE. Results: Negative-affect EE (N-EE) has been linked to changes in food choice, diet quality, processing degree, eating patterns, and potential abdominal adiposity, but these associations do not resolve the contentious question of whether EE is a distinct clinical entity. Eating in response to emotional states has also been linked to depression, emotion dysregulation, dietary restraint, binge eating, body-image concerns, sleep disturbance, and obesity-related outcomes. However, these associations are heterogeneous and do not define a unique disorder. One important asymmetry further complicates classification: N-EE is more consistently associated with psychopathology, while positive EE (P-EE) often occurs in normative social contexts. The proposed framework positions EE as a dimensional, transdiagnostic phenotype and identifies convergent multimethod validity, clinically meaningful thresholds, and discriminant, longitudinal, nutritional, prognostic, and treatment validity beyond established eating and mood disorders as requirements for potential categorical recognition. Conclusions: The literature considered suggests that EE may be usefully approached as a dimensional, transdiagnostic nutritional-behavioral phenotype. This remains a provisional conceptual position rather than an empirically validated classification. Further multimethod and longitudinal research is needed to clarify clinical significance, diagnostic boundaries, and utility before considering independent diagnostic recognition.

papers.title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
papers.abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

papers.title: Effects of Circadian Phase and Exercise Training on Systemic and Tissue-Specific Redox Responses in Mice Fed a High-Fat Diet.
papers.abstract: The effects of exercise timing on redox adaptation under high-fat diet (HFD)-induced metabolic stress remain unclear. We investigated whether the circadian phase of training alters systemic and tissue-specific redox responses in HFD-fed mice. Male C57BL/6J mice fed an HFD remained sedentary or underwent 8 weeks of treadmill training at Zeitgeber time 3 (ZT3) or Zeitgeber time 15 (ZT15). Samples were collected 48 h after the final session. Plasma redox status was assessed using the OXY-adsorbent test (OXY), the derivatives of reactive oxygen metabolites test (d-ROMs; mainly reflecting circulating hydroperoxides), and the biological antioxidant potential test (BAP), and redox and inflammatory gene expression levels were quantified in three skeletal muscles and the liver. Exercise increased BAP (p = 0.0442), whereas OXY was unchanged. The phase × exercise interaction for d-ROMs showed a nonsignificant trend (p = 0.0560); exploratory comparisons showed higher d-ROMs in ZT15-sedentary (sed) than in ZT3-sed and ZT15-exercise (exe) mice. Gastrocnemius (GAS) Nfe2l2 showed a nominal phase × exercise interaction. Soleus (SOL) Hmox1 was higher at ZT15 and with exercise. Quadriceps (QUA) Nfe2l2 was higher at ZT3 and Cat at ZT15. Hepatic Keap1 was higher at ZT15, particularly in sedentary mice, while inflammatory transcripts remained largely unchanged. Only the phase effects on SOL Hmox1 and hepatic Keap1 remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Long-term exercise was associated with higher plasma ferric-reducing capacity irrespective of circadian phase, whereas tissue redox-related transcriptional responses were mainly associated with circadian phase and differed among tissues. Whether active-phase exercise provides a redox advantage over rest-phase exercise requires further investigation.

papers.title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults. In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity. At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred. L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

papers.title: When Genetics Meets the Mediterranean Diet Across Metabolic Diseases.
papers.abstract: Metabolic diseases and related cardiometabolic conditions, including type 2 diabetes (T2D), obesity, metabolic syndrome (MetS), and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), arise from complex interactions between genetic predisposition and environmental factors. Among dietary patterns, the Mediterranean diet (MedDiet) has consistently been associated with improved metabolic health and a reduced risk of cardiometabolic diseases. However, substantial interindividual variability in metabolic responses to dietary exposures suggests that genetic susceptibility may contribute to differences in response to the MedDiet. Over the past two decades, nutrigenetic research has investigated whether adherence to the MedDiet can modify the effects of genetic variants associated with metabolic risk. Initial studies focused primarily on candidate genes involved in glucose metabolism, adiposity regulation, circadian rhythms, and hepatic lipid metabolism, including variants in genes such as TCF7L2, FTO, CLOCK, ADIPOQ, and PNPLA3. More recently, research has expanded to genetic risk score and polygenic risk score approaches, providing a broader assessment of inherited susceptibility. This literature review summarizes current evidence on MedDiet-gene interactions in T2D, obesity, MetS, MASLD, and related cardiometabolic traits, highlighting the transition from candidate-gene approaches to aggregate genetic risk models. Overall, the available literature suggests that the beneficial effects of the MedDiet are observed across different levels of genetic susceptibility, whereas evidence supporting clinically relevant gene-diet interactions remains heterogeneous and limited. Further large-scale, multi-ancestry, and well-designed prospective studies are needed before genetically tailored MedDiet recommendations can be routinely implemented in clinical practice.

papers.title: Dietary and Lifestyle Correlates of Gut Microbiota Diversity and Composition in Healthy Adults: A Cross-Sectional Pilot Study Informing Longitudinal Research.
papers.abstract: Modifiable dietary and lifestyle factors may contribute to gut microbiota variation but are often evaluated separately. This pilot study examined four exposures across complementary microbiome domains and used association magnitude and uncertainty to inform longitudinal study design. Twenty healthy adults (10 females and 10 males) provided a fresh-stool specimen and completed the exposure questionnaire on the day of specimen production. Exposures comprised Mediterranean diet adherence, ultra-processed food consumption frequency, physical activity, and sleep characteristics. Microbiome outcomes comprised independently recalculated OTU-level Shannon diversity (primary outcome) and Pielou's evenness, genus-level Bray-Curtis and Aitchison distances, centered log-ratio coordinates of eight prespecified genera, and the natural-log-transformed Prevotella/Bacteroides ratio. Associations were evaluated using age- and sex-adjusted linear regression and permutational multivariate analysis of variance, with false-discovery-rate control, influence diagnostics, and robustness analyses. Scenario-based sample-size calculations were restricted to age- and sex-adjusted cross-sectional linear regression models. Complete exposure and microbiome data were available for all participants. No association was supported after false-discovery-rate correction. However, the observed effect estimates were not uniformly negligible: maximum partial R2 values were 0.140 across the alpha-diversity models, 0.210 for the UPF-Akkermansia association, and 0.108 for the Prevotella/Bacteroides log-ratio, whereas the maximum marginal R2 for overall community composition was 0.0649. Estimates were imprecise and participant-sensitive, and robustness analyses did not alter the overall interpretation. Conservative scenarios for age- and sex-adjusted cross-sectional regression models, based on assumed partial R2 values of 0.03-0.05, yielded planning benchmarks of 275-465 analyzable participants, or 306-582 enrolled participants assuming 10-20% unusable observations. This pilot does not establish the absence of diet-microbiota or lifestyle-microbiota relationships. Instead, it provides a reproducible framework for prioritizing hypotheses and planning adequately powered longitudinal studies using repeated, temporally aligned exposure and microbiome measurements.

papers.title: Mediterranean Diet Adherence and Sleep Quality in Spanish Adults: Divergent Associations Between Subjective and Objective Measures.
papers.abstract: Objective: We aimed to examine the association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet (MD) and sleep quality assessed using both subjective and objective methods in a general adult population. Design: This is a cross-sectional study. Adherence to the MD was evaluated using the Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener, while sleep quality was assessed subjectively using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and objectively using wrist actigraphy over five consecutive days. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were applied, adjusting for key sociodemographic and clinical confounders. Settings: We investigated a general adult population from Spain with a total of 500 Spanish adults aged 25-65 years. Results: Higher MEDAS scores were significantly associated with better subjective sleep quality. Each one-point increase in MD adherence was associated with lower PSQI scores, and participants with higher adherence had lower odds of poor sleep quality, although this association did not reach statistical significance. Cluster analysis identified a dietary pattern characterized by higher consumption of fruits, vegetables, fish and olive oil that was associated with better perceived sleep quality. No significant associations were observed between MD adherence and objective sleep parameters, including sleep efficiency, sleep fragmentation or wake after sleep onset. Conclusions: Greater adherence to the MD was associated with better perceived sleep quality but not with objectively measured sleep parameters. These findings suggest that dietary patterns may influence sleep perception rather than objective sleep characteristics and highlight the potential role of the MD as a modifiable factor related to sleep-related well-being.

papers.title: Probing Melatonin's Release Pattern from Oral Solid Dosage Forms Using Synthetic Biopolymers.
papers.abstract: Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) (MLT) is a naturally occurring hormone produced endogenously, primarily in the suprachiasmatic nucleus. MLT exhibits a plethora of uses particularly in the treatment of sleep disorders (sleep onset and maintenance). However, due to its short biological half-life, MLT cannot maintain effective plasma concentrations for a prolonged period when it is exogenously taken from immediate-release formulations. The present study aims at developing modified release systems capable of gradually releasing MLT, thereby sustaining its pharmacological effect over eight hours. To this end, modified-release tablets were prepared using new polymeric excipients based on polylactic acid (PLA). Both neat PLA and PLA copolymers with polyethylene glycols (PEGs) of varying molecular weights (PLLA-PEG-PLLA_4000, PLLA-PEG-PLLA_6000, and PLLA-PEG-PLLA_8000) were used, along with other excipients. Certain formulations delivered MLT comparatively fast and may therefore be useful for sleep onset problems, others matched the release behaviour of the marketed product Circadin®, and the rest released the hormone in a more prolonged manner.

papers.title: Dissociation Between Symptom Burden and Structural Pathology in Patients Undergoing Upper Gastrointestinal Endoscopy: A Retrospective Single-Center Study Using Latent Class Analysis.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Upper gastrointestinal symptoms often correspond poorly with endoscopic and histological pathology. We aimed to identify lifestyle and psychosocial phenotypes and examine their clinical features, objective findings, and symptom-pathology concordance. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included adults undergoing outpatient upper gastrointestinal endoscopy at a tertiary gastroenterology center in Latvia between 1 May and 31 December 2025. Latent class analysis was applied to questionnaire-derived lifestyle, behavioral, anthropometric, and psychosocial indicators. Classes were subsequently characterized using clinical features, endoscopic findings, and histology. Additional analyses assessed potential confounding by age and sex and exploratory predictive discrimination. Results: The cohort included 2192 patients, of whom 1755 had histology. A three-class solution had the lowest mean Bayesian Information Criterion, with substantial agreement across 20 imputed datasets. Class 1 (46.9%) combined high psychosocial burden with comparatively low substance exposure. Class 2 (12.0%) combined greater substance exposure with high psychosocial burden and the highest anxiety prevalence. Class 3 (41.0%) exhibited lower psychosocial burden, less prolonged sitting, fewer patients with short sleep duration, and the highest combined prevalence of overweight and obesity. The clinical feature composite showed limited diagnostic performance, and correlations between clinical feature burden and pathology burdens were negligible (Spearman's ρ = -0.012 to 0.026; all p > 0.05). Clinical feature-dominant discordance was most frequent in Class 2 (25.5%), whereas pathology-dominant discordance was most frequent in Class 3 (29.7%). Eleven clinical-feature associations remained significant after age and sex adjustment and false discovery rate correction; no overall associations with individual endoscopic or histological findings met this threshold. Exploratory ROC analyses showed limited discrimination. Conclusions: The phenotypes demonstrated distinct patterns of symptom-pathology dissociation. Lifestyle-based phenotyping provides a framework for characterizing this heterogeneity, while its clinical application requires validation in independent populations.

papers.title: Association Between Sleep Duration and Obesity Phenotypes in Apparently Healthy Korean Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study Using the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2013-2015.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Evidence on the association between sleep duration and obesity phenotypes jointly considering adiposity and metabolic health is limited, particularly in adults without known chronic diseases. We aimed to examine this association in apparently healthy Korean adults. Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed 7808 apparently healthy adults aged ≥20 years from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2013-2015, assigned to metabolically healthy normal weight (MHNW), metabolically abnormal normal weight (MANW), metabolically healthy obesity (MHO), or metabolically abnormal obesity (MAO) phenotypes. Self-reported sleep duration was grouped as ≤5, 6, 7, 8, or ≥9 h/day. Survey-weighted multinomial logistic regression was performed with MHNW and ≥9 h as references, adjusting for age and sex (Model 1) and socioeconomic and lifestyle factors (Model 2). Sensitivity analyses used 7 h/day as the reference and a stricter definition of metabolic health; effect modification by sex and age was examined. Results: The proportion of MHNW increased from 61.6% (≤5 h) to 76.0% (≥9 h) (p < 0.001). In Model 2, sleeping ≤5 h was associated with higher odds of MHO (odds ratio [OR] 1.380, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.098-1.734) and MAO (OR 1.472, 95% CI 1.109-1.953) relative to 7 h, and these associations remained significant after false discovery rate correction, whereas none of the associations relative to ≥9 h, including that with MANW, did. Under the stricter definition, the association with MAO persisted, whereas that with MHO was no longer statistically significant despite a similar effect estimate (vs. 7 h: OR 1.394, 95% CI 0.926-2.098); no significant interactions by sex or age were observed for MHO or MAO. Conclusions: In apparently healthy Korean adults, short sleep duration was associated with higher odds of MHO and MAO, most consistently MAO, but not robustly with MANW. Because of the cross-sectional design, these associations do not imply causality, and prospective studies are needed to determine whether sleep duration is a modifiable target for metabolic health.

papers.title: A Multidisciplinary Care Pathway for Childhood Mouth Breathing: The Pediatric Allergist, ENT, and Orthodontic Perspective.
papers.abstract: Background: Mouth breathing (MB) in children is a functional alteration characterized by the substitution of nasal breathing with oral or mixed breathing. Persistent MB, particularly when occurring during sleep (nocturnal MB), may be associated with sleep fragmentation, neurobehavioral disturbances, and alterations in craniofacial development. Although established sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), particularly obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS), is well-recognized and addressed by international guidelines, children presenting with persistent or nocturnal MB without established diagnostic criteria for OSAS may remain outside conventional diagnostic pathways. The multifactorial nature of MB therefore requires the coordinated evaluation of nasal, allergic, upper airway, craniofacial, dental, and orofacial factors. Methods: This narrative review was based primarily on a structured search of the PubMed/MEDLINE database covering publications from database inception to June 2026, supplemented by manual screening of the reference lists of relevant articles and clinical guidelines. The literature was selected according to relevance to the review objectives, methodological robustness, clinical applicability, and contribution to pediatric, allergological, otorhinolaryngological, and dental/orthodontic perspectives. Priority was given to systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, clinical practice guidelines, consensus documents, and high-quality observational studies. A total of 79 references were included in the final manuscript. Results: The reviewed evidence indicates that MB may be associated with allergic and nasal conditions, upper airway obstruction, craniofacial and dental abnormalities, and orofacial functional alterations, and may coexist with SDB in selected children. The evidence was synthesized across pediatric, allergological, otorhinolaryngological, and orthodontic perspectives to develop a multidisciplinary care pathway based on the clinical identification of MB, targeted specialist assessment, objective evaluation of SDB when indicated, and individualized management and follow-up. Conclusions: MB may represent an important clinical entry point for the early recognition of potentially treatable conditions and associated SDB. The proposed multidisciplinary care pathway integrates pediatric, allergological, otorhinolaryngological, and dental/orthodontic expertise to support coordinated assessment, individualized management, and longitudinal follow-up of children with MB.

papers.title: Menopausal Symptom Burden and Self-Reported Poor Sleep Quality Among Japanese Working Women Aged 40 Years and Older: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep-related complaints are common among women in midlife and may reflect not only insufficient sleep duration but also broader menopausal symptom burden. Although menopausal symptoms and sleep problems are known to be related, less is known about how menopausal symptom domains are associated with self-reported sleep quality among working women, particularly when objective sleep duration is considered. This exploratory cross-sectional study aimed to examine the association between menopausal symptom burden and self-reported poor sleep quality among Japanese working women aged 40 years and older, while accounting for objectively measured sleep duration. Materials and Methods: Participants completed questionnaires on sleep quality and menopausal symptoms and underwent objective sleep monitoring using a wearable electroencephalography device. Self-reported sleep quality was assessed using an item corresponding to the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and dichotomized into poor and good sleep quality. Menopausal symptoms were evaluated using the Simplified Menopausal Index, including vasomotor, psychological, and somatic domains, with higher scores indicating greater symptom burden. Results: Among 79 participants, 43 reported poor sleep quality and 36 reported good sleep quality. Women with poor sleep quality had higher total and domain-specific SMI scores and shorter objective sleep duration. In logistic regression analyses adjusted for age and objective sleep duration, total SMI score and each symptom domain were associated with poor sleep quality. These associations remained significant in sensitivity analyses excluding the sleep-related SMI item from the total score and psychological domain score. Conclusions: Self-reported poor sleep quality among Japanese working women aged 40 years and older may reflect menopausal symptom burden beyond objectively measured sleep duration. The consistency of the findings across sensitivity analyses supports the robustness of this association. Sleep complaints may therefore serve as an accessible signal for recognizing menopausal symptom burden in clinical and occupational health settings.

papers.title: Clinical Outcomes of Combined Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty and All-Suture Anchor Tongue Base Suspension for Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: All-suture anchor tongue base suspension (TBS) is a recently introduced approach that provides mandibular fixation without a permanent metallic anchor body. Clinical outcome data for this technique when incorporated into multilevel surgery remain limited. This study evaluated clinical outcomes and postoperative complications following multilevel surgery incorporating all-suture anchor TBS in adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-arm observational study included 30 of 40 consecutive adults with polysomnography-confirmed moderate-to-severe OSA who were intolerant of or declined continuous positive airway pressure therapy and had complete postoperative polysomnography and at least 6 months of follow-up. All patients underwent uvulopalatopharyngoplasty combined with all-suture anchor TBS. Preoperative and 6-month postoperative assessments included the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), nadir oxygen saturation, Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), snoring visual analog scale (VAS), and body mass index (BMI). Results: Median AHI decreased from 50.5 (Q1-Q3, 38.0-68.0) to 15.7 (Q1-Q3, 11.1-21.4) events/h (p < 0.001). ESS improved from 16.3 ± 2.5 to 7.5 ± 2.4 (p < 0.01), and nadir oxygen saturation increased from 68.5% ± 6.5% to 82.8% ± 9.2% (p < 0.01). Surgical success was achieved in 22 patients (73%). Complications were predominantly mild and transient; no infection, suture rupture, or permanent functional deficit occurred. Conclusions: Multilevel surgery incorporating all-suture anchor TBS was associated with significant improvements in objective and subjective sleep outcomes at 6 months, with predominantly mild and transient complications. These findings support the feasibility of incorporating this technique into a multilevel surgical protocol; comparative studies are needed to determine the specific contribution of TBS.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Screening for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Using Photographic Craniofacial and Speech-Derived Acoustic Features.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a prevalent disorder for which accessible non-invasive screening approaches remain of interest. This study evaluated photographic craniofacial descriptors and speech-derived acoustic features for Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) estimation and binary OSA screening. Data from 109 adults were analyzed using unsegmented and temporally segmented speech representations. Seven craniofacial, acoustic, and combined feature configurations were evaluated using nested cross-validation. For regression, the lowest MAE was 14.242 events/h using segmented continuous-speech features with Random Forest. For classification, the highest AUC-ROC was 0.766 using unsegmented craniofacial features with a multilayer perceptron classifier, while the best segmented result was 0.756 using craniofacial plus continuous-speech features. Craniofacial-only features in the segmented representation achieved a similar AUC-ROC of 0.753, indicating no clear discriminative advantage from adding acoustic features. Several classifiers showed high sensitivity but comparatively low specificity. Sensitivity analysis excluding the four participants with the highest AHI values showed similar classification patterns, although regression performance was more sensitive to cohort composition. Overall, craniofacial descriptors provided the most consistent predictive contribution, whereas acoustic features showed model- and representation-dependent value for OSA screening.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythm and Lipid Metabolism: The Role of the Gut Microbiota.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms play a vital role in lipid metabolism by coordinating lipogenesis, lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation to maintain energy homeostasis. Their regulation is affected by light exposure, feeding time, dietary composition, hormonal signals and gut microbiota. Accordingly, persistent circadian misalignment may therefore increase susceptibility to obesity and related metabolic disorders. Increasing evidence also indicates that the gut microbiota exhibits marked diurnal variation and can, in turn, modulate host metabolic rhythms through microbial metabolites and host-microbe signaling. This review summarizes the major factors influencing circadian rhythms, discusses their regulatory effects on lipid metabolism and the contribution of the gut microbiota, and outlines the relationship between circadian disruption and obesity, with the aim of providing insights into the prevention and intervention of metabolic diseases.

papers.title: The Relationship Between Sleep Quality and Shooting Accuracy in Female Archers: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Precision sports such as archery require sustained attention, fine motor control, and technical consistency, all of which may be influenced by sleep quality. This cross-sectional study aimed to examine the association between sleep quality and shooting accuracy in female archers and to determine whether this association persisted after adjustment for age and sport experience. Twenty-six female archers (mean age: 21.23 ± 2.35 years) participated in the study. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and shooting accuracy (%) was calculated by normalizing the total score according to the number of shots performed. Associations between PSQI total score and shooting accuracy were examined using Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses and linear regression models. The mean PSQI total score was 6.15 ± 1.95, and the mean shooting accuracy was 77.69 ± 13.26%. Neither Pearson (r = 0.168, p = 0.413, BCa 95% CI [-0.222, 0.505]) nor Spearman correlation (ρ = 0.043, p = 0.835, BCa 95% CI [-0.343, 0.426]) showed a statistically significant association between PSQI total score and shooting accuracy. The adjusted regression model including age and sport experience was also not statistically significant (R2 = 0.032, F(3, 22) = 0.24, p = 0.866), and PSQI total score was not significantly associated with shooting accuracy after adjustment (B = 1.11, β = 0.163, p = 0.447, 95% CI [-1.86, 4.07]). In this sample of female archers, no statistically significant association was detected between habitual sleep quality assessed by the PSQI and shooting accuracy. Given the small sample size and the wide confidence intervals, larger prospective studies incorporating objective and session-specific sleep measures are needed to clarify the relationship between sleep quality and precision performance in archery.

papers.title: Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea Is Associated with Cholesterol Target Non-Attainment in Patients Undergoing Cardiac Surgery: A Secondary Analysis of a Prospective Observational Cohort.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) has been associated with adverse cardiometabolic profiles, but its relationship with cholesterol target attainment in patients receiving lipid-lowering therapy remains incompletely characterized. We investigated the association between severe OSA and non-attainment of predefined cholesterol thresholds in patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery. This secondary analysis included 142 adults from a prospectively assembled observational cohort. Participants underwent in-hospital preoperative Type III cardiorespiratory polygraphy, fasting lipid assessment, and documentation of lipid-lowering therapy. Severe OSA was defined as an apnea-hypopnea index ≥30 events/h. The primary outcome was non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (non-HDL-C) ≥ 100 mg/dL. Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, diabetes mellitus, high-intensity statin therapy, and non-statin lipid-lowering therapy. Severe OSA was associated with higher odds of non-HDL-C ≥ 100 mg/dL (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 3.49, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.56-7.78; p = 0.002), LDL-C ≥ 55 mg/dL (OR 2.93, 95% CI 1.18-7.29; p = 0.021), and LDL-C ≥ 70 mg/dL (OR 2.30, 95% CI 1.03-5.12; p = 0.041). In contrast, associations with continuous LDL-C (p = 0.113) and non-HDL-C (p = 0.100) concentrations were not statistically significant. No significant associations were observed for triglyceride-related or lipid-derived outcomes. The primary association with non-HDL-C ≥ 100 mg/dL remained significant in the analysis restricted to statin-treated patients. Severe OSA was associated with non-attainment of predefined cholesterol thresholds in this cardiac surgical cohort, with the strongest and most consistent association observed for non-HDL-C ≥ 100 mg/dL. These findings identify an association with categorical cholesterol target non-attainment but do not establish treatment failure, causality, or a generalized increase in cholesterol concentrations.

papers.title: The Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care Ecosystem in the United States: Clinical Pathways and the Evolving Role of Otolaryngology.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common, heterogeneous disorder managed through a multidisciplinary pathway that connects recognition, physiologic testing, treatment selection, specialty referral, insurance coverage, and longitudinal reassessment. This narrative review provides a clinically oriented, system-level overview of the adult OSA care ecosystem in the United States for an international clinical audience, with particular emphasis on the evolving role of otolaryngology. We describe the organization and complementary functions of sleep physicians, otolaryngologists, dentists, and allied health professionals. We also outline the roles of polysomnography and home sleep apnea testing, along with major therapeutic pathways including positive airway pressure, oral appliance therapy, weight management, upper-airway surgery, and neurostimulation. Otolaryngology provides an important interface between physiologic diagnosis and airway-specific treatment by integrating anatomic evaluation, sleep-state airway phenotyping, intervention selection, and post-treatment reassessment. Recent advances in neurostimulation, pharmacologic weight management, wearable and home-based monitoring, airflow analysis, and artificial intelligence are expanding opportunities for accessible and phenotype-informed care. Important challenges include underdiagnosis, treatment attrition, fragmented transitions, variable coverage, and reliance on the apnea-hypopnea index. Although health-care structures differ internationally, multidisciplinary coordination, individualized treatment selection, and longitudinal reassessment provide broadly applicable principles for developing patient-centered OSA programs.

papers.title: Prevalence of Chronic Respiratory Diseases, Airflow Obstruction, Sleep Apnea Risk, and Novel Tobacco Use in the Coastal Localities of the Mangalia Municipality: A Cross-Sectional Study of 979 Adults.
papers.abstract: Spirometric airflow obstruction frequently remains unrecognised in community settings, representing a major diagnostic gap in chronic respiratory disease management. Population-based epidemiological data from Romanian coastal communities-characterised by a highly dynamic population including residents, seasonal workers, and tourists-remain scarce. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of screening-detected pre-bronchodilator airflow obstruction and chronic respiratory diseases, characterise smoking behaviours including novel tobacco product use, identify individuals at elevated risk for sleep apnea, and examine patterns of preventive care and healthcare utilisation across five Black Sea coastal localities. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 979 adults from five coastal localities in Constanța County, Romania, as part of a community-based respiratory screening campaign conducted 11-16 August 2025: Neptun (n = 147), Olimp (n = 178), Saturn (n = 187), Mangalia (n = 257), and Jupiter (n = 210). Data were collected using a structured questionnaire covering 22 domains, including medical diagnoses, spirometric measurements (FEV1/FVC%), sleep quality, snoring, anthropometric parameters, comorbidities, and healthcare utilisation. Airflow obstruction was defined as an FEV1/FVC ratio < 70%. The primary outcome of interest was the prevalence of screening-detected pre-bronchodilator airflow obstruction, including among individuals without a prior respiratory diagnosis. Sleep apnea risk was defined by the co-reporting of habitual snoring and witnessed apneic episodes, used as a two-item screening proxy. Among 979 participants (51.4% female; mean age 47.3 ± 13.5 years), 9.3% had at least one CRD: asthma (4.4%), chronic bronchitis (3.0%), COPD (1.7%), and emphysema (0.3%). CRD prevalence increased with age, from 6.1% in individuals <40 years to 24.2% in those aged 71-80 years. Of 973 participants with spirometry data, 17.9% demonstrated airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC < 70%), including 15.7% without a prior respiratory diagnosis, representing previously unrecognised airflow limitation rather than confirmed chronic disease. Screening-defined OSA-risk positivity, based on a two-item proxy of habitual snoring and witnessed apnoeic episodes, was identified in 10.9% (n = 107) and was more common among obese participants (19.5% vs. 7.9%; absolute difference 11.6 percentage points; p < 0.001). Current smoking was reported by 35.2%, and 8.9% reported the use of novel tobacco products. Influenza vaccination coverage was 20.0%, while pneumococcal vaccination uptake was 3.4%. One in six adults without a prior respiratory diagnosis demonstrated spirometric airflow limitation, suggesting that opportunistic spirometry in primary care could substantially improve case detection in Romanian coastal communities. OSA risk, assessed by symptom-based screening proxy, was present in 10.9% of participants, with higher BMI as the strongest independent predictor among the variables assessed. High smoking prevalence (35.2%) and critically low pneumococcal vaccination coverage (3.4%) represent additional modifiable public health targets. These findings support a unified community respiratory screening approach incorporating spirometry, sleep apnea risk stratification, and vaccination audit, particularly in primary care settings serving coastal populations with dynamic demographics.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing: Key Pathophysiological Mechanisms and Their Clinical Implications.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) encompasses a spectrum of conditions characterized by abnormal respiratory patterns during sleep. These disorders include obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), central sleep apnea (CSA), hypoventilation syndromes, primary snoring, and upper airway resistance syndrome (UARS). These disorders disrupt normal sleep architecture, contributing to sleep fragmentation, impaired daytime function, and significant cardiometabolic morbidity. This review synthesizes current understanding of the physiologic mechanisms underlying SDB, beginning with normal sleep regulation and extending to disease-specific pathophysiology. By integrating pathophysiological mechanisms with their clinical implications, this review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding disease heterogeneity and progression. The goal of this review is to provide clinicians with the resources to inform more precise diagnoses, patient classifications, and treatment strategies for sleep-disordered breathing. OSA is characterized by repetitive upper airway collapse, which can be further characterized by emerging phenotypes and endotypes that highlight heterogeneity in the clinical presentation and polysomnographic features. CSA, in contrast, results from diminished or absent respiratory drive and is frequently associated with heightened chemoreflex sensitivity and ventilatory instability. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome represents a severe form of SDB marked by impaired respiratory mechanics, reduced lung compliance, and blunted ventilatory drive, partly mediated by leptin resistance. Primary snoring and Upper Airway Resistance syndrome exist along a continuum of increasing airway resistance and collapsibility, with emerging evidence suggesting these conditions may not be entirely benign. Additionally, there may be overlaps between diagnoses with patients meeting the criteria for multiple. Classification of SDB has evolved through integration of clinical features, polysomnographic parameters, and pathophysiologic mechanisms.

papers.title: A Multi-Integrated Approach to Tinnitus Phenotype-Guided Otolaryngological, Dental, and Physiotherapeutic Care.
papers.abstract: Background: Tinnitus is a heterogeneous percept that becomes a disorder when it is accompanied by clinically meaningful distress or functional impairment. Hearing loss is a major contributor, while temporomandibular, cervical, sleep, psychological, and contextual factors can shape symptom expression. This heterogeneity supports coordinated assessment, but it does not by itself prove that an integrated care pathway improves outcomes. Objective: To narratively synthesize evidence relevant to phenotype-guided tinnitus care and to propose a clinical-organizational framework for coordinating otolaryngological and audiological care, dental and temporomandibular management, physiotherapeutic rehabilitation, and complementary behavioral and sleep interventions. Methods: A structured narrative review was developed with reference to SANRA. PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, major guideline repositories, and targeted citation searches were examined for English-language evidence from January 2014 to 12 August 2026, with seminal earlier publications retained. Guidelines, systematic reviews, randomized trials, and clinically informative observational studies were prioritized. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized thematically rather than pooled. Results: The evidence separates into three levels. Guideline-supported or relatively strong evidence underpins diagnostic assessment, education, cognitive behavioral therapy, and hearing rehabilitation when indicated. Temporomandibular and cervical interventions have more limited, phenotype-specific evidence from small and heterogeneous studies. No comparative study has validated the proposed integrated framework as a complete treatment package. We therefore present coordination, phenotype-gated referral, shared outcomes, and explicit adaptation or stop rules as a hypothesis-generating organizational model. Conclusions: The proposed framework should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating organizational model rather than a validated treatment package. Its individual components retain their own levels of evidence, and prospective studies should compare the coordinated framework with usual or standard care using both clinical and health-economic outcomes.

papers.title: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia and MASLD in Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Critical Appraisal of Mechanistic and Causal Evidence.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) frequently coexist and share a common cardiometabolic substrate through a shared cardiometabolic substrate. This narrative review critically appraises the epidemiological, experimental, and interventional evidence proposed to link chronic intermittent hypoxia (CIH) and sleep fragmentation to hepatic steatosis, steatohepatitis, and fibrosis. We summarize the candidate mechanisms, including mitochondrial oxidative stress, hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha signaling, sympathetically driven lipolysis, and Kupffer and stellate cell activation and then examine the limits of the evidence supporting them: hypoxia-induced hypophagia and the scarcity of pair-fed controls in rodent models, species differences in the physiological response to hypoxia, publication bias, common-cause confounding by age and systemic inflammation, and the rarity of progressive liver disease in lean patients with anatomically driven OSA. We further review non-invasive diagnostic tools, polysomnographic hypoxemia indices, transient elastography, METS-IR, FIB-4, and emerging biomarkers, such as omentin-1 and follistatin-like 1, that enable bidirectional screening between sleep and hepatology clinics. Finally, we discuss therapeutic strategies, including continuous positive airway pressure, structured weight loss, and incretin-based pharmacotherapy (GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists), highlighting recent phase 3 evidence for tirzepatide in OSA and semaglutide in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. Current evidence supports CIH as a context-dependent amplifier of liver injury in patients with pre-existing metabolic dysfunction rather than as an established independent cause of MASH. This interpretation still justifies integrated screening and treatment pathways, while identifying the study designs needed to test causality directly.

papers.title: The Sedentary-Stress Paradox in Esports: Neuroendocrine, Metabolic, and Endothelial Pathways to Cardiovascular Risk.
papers.abstract: Esports and gaming resemble traditional sports and physical activity because both involve sustained cognitive and emotional stress; however, this stress occurs against a background of prolonged sedentary behavior. This narrative review examines the neuroendocrine, metabolic, and endothelial consequences of this "stress without movement" phenotype and its potential implications for long-term cardiovascular health. Activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system disrupts sleep and circadian rhythms. Continuous neuroendocrine activation may impair muscle-adipose tissue crosstalk and nitric oxide-dependent endothelial function. Although direct longitudinal evidence linking gaming to cardiovascular disease is currently lacking, these convergent mechanisms identify prolonged sedentary gaming as a potential cardiovascular risk amplifier, particularly when combined with occupational sitting, sleep disruption, adiposity, and other cardiometabolic risk factors.

papers.title: The Glymphatic-Meningeal Lymphatic System and Autophagy in ME/CFS and Long COVID: A Mechanistic Perspective.
papers.abstract: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Long COVID) are complex multisystem disorders affecting 60-400 million individuals globally. They are considered post-infectious illnesses and share similar biological mechanisms, including immune dysregulation, orthostatic intolerance and cognitive dysfunction, highlighting a substantial overlap between the two conditions. Persistent fatigue, sleep dysfunction, post-exertional malaise and brain fog are among some of their most common and debilitating symptoms. Despite extensive research, they remain incurable, with no effective treatments, or simple diagnostic tests. They are increasingly understood as heterogeneous, multisystem diseases, involving neurological symptoms, with varying severities and diverse underlying biological abnormalities. More recently, the possibility of glymphatic dysfunction and autophagy impairment have been proposed as parts of the mechanistic features of the pathophysiology of these conditions, which are discussed more fully in the present perspective. With the glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic systems being operationally integrated, we will try to delineate how the metabolic waste removal mechanism afforded by this system may work together with autophagy to maintain brain homeostasis. We will provide some of the established mechanistic features of toxicity of misfolded proteins, explore their role in causing glymphatic dysfunction and impairing autophagy, and discuss the potential for therapeutic interventions.

papers.title: Salivary Melatonin Levels in Comparison with Disease Features and Antihistamine Use: Prospective Follow-Up of Atopic Dermatitis Patients.
papers.abstract: Background: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common inflammatory dermatosis often accompanied by itching and sleep disturbances. Various treatment options exist, including antihistamines (AHs), even though current clinical recommendations do not mention them. Methods: This prospective exploratory study measured and recorded salivary melatonin at two timepoints (T1 and T2) in three groups of participants: those not treated with AHs, those who discontinued H1-AHs, and those for whom H1-AHs were introduced. Also assessed were disease severity (Scoring Atopic Dermatitis/SCORAD and Eczema Area and Severity Index/EASI), pruritus severity (Peak Pruritus Numeric Rating Scale/NRS), and sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index/PSQI). Results: The EASI scores were significantly inversely correlated with salivary melatonin levels (p = 0.009) at the first timepoint (T1), but not at the second timepoint (T2). At T2, SCORAD correlated with EASI, NRS, and PSQI (ρ = 0.304-0.842; p ≤ 0.022). EASI correlated with NRS and PSQI (ρ = 0.281-0.453; p ≤ 0.035). Those who discontinued AHs showed increased AD severity indicators (SCORAD, EASI, NRS), whereas participants for whom AHs were introduced showed decreases in the same scores. After adjusting for baseline values, a significant main effect was detected for the treatment group for T2 SCORAD scores (p < 0.001, η2 = 0.493). Pairwise comparisons confirmed significant differences among all treatment arms/measures (all p values ≤ 0.023). Changes in melatonin levels between the three groups were not significant when baseline SCORAD values were controlled for. Conclusions: Our exploratory study observed an inverse association between melatonin levels and AD severity at T1, but this was not replicated at T2. This association should be interpreted with caution due to study limitations. Changes in AD severity and pruritus scores following AH initiation or discontinuation were observed, but the study's non-randomized design and baseline differences between groups preclude a definitive causal inference, and further research on this topic is needed.

papers.title: The Interplay Between Pediatric Atopic Dermatitis and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Emerging Evidence, Mechanistic Insights, and Clinical Implications.
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease in children and is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder with potential consequences beyond the skin. Growing evidence links pediatric AD to neurodevelopmental disorders, particularly attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but the mechanisms and clinical implications remain incompletely understood. Systemic and neuroimmune inflammation, altered T-helper-cell and cytokine signaling, and genetic and epigenetic susceptibility may contribute to this association. Sleep disruption and psychosocial stress represent additional potential pathways linking skin inflammation with neurodevelopment. Stronger associations have been reported in children with severe or early-onset AD, multiple atopic comorbidities, and persistent sleep disturbance, highlighting the importance of disease heterogeneity. This narrative review integrates epidemiologic evidence and proposed mechanisms to examine the skin-brain axis in pediatric AD, with particular attention to high-risk phenotypes and implications for developmental surveillance and multidisciplinary management. Although current evidence supports an association, causality remains uncertain. Prospective studies integrating AD phenotypes, biomarkers, and neurodevelopmental assessments are needed to clarify these relationships and determine whether early effective AD treatment can modify long-term neurodevelopmental trajectories.

papers.title: Atopic Dermatitis in the Era of Exposome and Artificial Intelligence.
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a heterogeneous, relapsing inflammatory skin disease in which epidermal barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, microbial imbalance, genetics, and the environment interact continuously over time. Although a substantial body of literature has linked AD with air pollution, weather, allergens, stress, infections, sleep disturbance, skin care practices and microbial perturbation, most studies have assessed single exposures in isolation. This reductionist approach only partially reflects the real-world biology of AD, where patients experience dynamic combinations of external and internal exposures whose effects are non-linear, cumulative and modified by age, phenotype, treatment and susceptibility. The exposome paradigm offers a broader conceptual lens by considering the totality of exposures over the life course. However, exposomic research in AD is methodologically challenging because the data are multimodal, high-dimensional, time-dependent, and often incomplete. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help address this complexity by integrating heterogeneous data layers, modelling temporal dependencies, discovering latent patterns, and generating individualized predictions. This narrative review examines current evidence and proposes a theoretical framework that integrates AI and the exposome in AD. We define the principal domains of the AD exposome, describe a multilevel analytical architecture spanning environmental, clinical, behavioural, microbiome, and multi-omics data. We distinguish applications evaluated in AD studies from exploratory analyses and proposed objectives: prediction of annual flare burden remains exploratory, whereas exposome-informed short-term flare alerts are proposed applications. Although selected AI applications have been evaluated in AD, the added predictive value of exposure data and the clinical utility of a fully integrated exposome-AI system remain to be established. We also outline key methodological and translational priorities, including exposure assessment, temporality, treatment-confounding, interpretability, fairness, data governance, and external validation. The proposed framework offers a structured basis for future research, with clinical translation dependent on prospective validation and evidence of benefit to patient care.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances and Circadian Phase Delay in People Living with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV): A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Advances in HIV research and antiretroviral therapy (ART) have substantially increased life expectancy among people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, challenges affecting quality of life and alterations in daily physiological processes persist. Among the health dimensions most affected are sleep quality and circadian rhythms, resulting in significant biological alterations. The main objective of this study is to analyze the existing scientific evidence regarding the effects of HIV on sleep quality and on the alignment and synchronization of circadian rhythms. The bidirectional interaction between these physiological alterations and associated clinical, immunological, and metabolic factors in people living with HIV (PLHIV) was evaluated, emphasizing their integration. For this review, searches were conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases. Eligibility criteria were applied, resulting in a final selection of 15 studies based on search strategies. The findings demonstrated a high prevalence of poor sleep quality as well as delayed circadian phase. These chronobiological alterations were closely associated with systemic inflammation, altered melatonin levels, impaired cognitive performance, and an altered metabolic profile involving leptin, ghrelin, adiponectin, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling. Despite the consistency of the results, the methodologies of individual studies varied, and a notable absence of clinical trials aimed at addressing poor sleep quality and chronodisruption was observed. A promising clinical approach involves complementing antiretroviral therapy (ART) with chronotherapeutic interventions and sleep hygiene. In conclusion, HIV can disrupt personal temporal organization at a systemic level; consequently, incorporating assessments of sleep and circadian rhythms into clinical care may be warranted, while chronotherapeutic interventions should be further investigated.

papers.title: Changes in Connexin-43 Expression and Neuropil Ultrastructure in the Cerebral Cortex of Bats During the Sleep-Wake Cycle.
papers.abstract: Sleep maintains central nervous system homeostasis, but many molecular mechanisms of sleep-wake regulation remain poorly understood. Connexin-43 (Cx43), the astrocytic gap junction protein, supports neuroglial communication, yet its role in physiological sleep is little studied. Here, we analyzed Cx43 expression, gap junction organization and neuropil ultrastructure in the motor cortex of common noctule bats (Nyctalus noctula) during sleep and wakefulness using confocal microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, semi-automated image analysis, and molecular dynamics. Sleep was associated with higher Cx43 immunoreactivity and with more and larger astrocytic gap-junction plaques than wakefulness. Across neuropil fields, synaptic, process and mitochondrial counts and total active-zone length were higher during wakefulness, and mean mitochondrial profiles were larger during sleep; after averaging within animals, only total active-zone length remained significantly greater during wakefulness. More perisynaptic astrocytic process (PAP) profiles contacted synapses during wakefulness, whereas individual PAPs were larger during sleep; both contrasts remained significant after animal-level averaging. As a secondary, hypothesis-generating analysis, we simulated histidine protonation of the Cx43 hemichannel as a simplified model of acidic conditions. Cerebral pH was not measured, and the simulations do not explain the sleep-associated Cx43 increase. In silico, protonation reduced conformational flexibility and narrowed the central and extracellular pore regions.

papers.title: The Fluid Percussion Injury Model of Traumatic Brain Injury: Insights into Post-Traumatic Epilepsy and Comorbidities.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) affects millions of people each year and can lead to persistent neurological disorders, including post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE). Animal models of concussion and TBI, developed since the late nineteenth century, provide a means to investigate injury progression and its consequences under controlled conditions. The lateral fluid percussion injury (LFPI) model is widely used to study both TBI and post-traumatic epileptogenesis. PTE is often resistant to antiseizure medications, and variability among experimental models (e.g., strain, injury, surgical, and physiological differences) remains a major obstacle to developing antiepileptogenic treatments. Understanding the factors that influence model reproducibility is therefore essential. This review first examines the development of the LFPI model and the experimental factors that influence PTE outcomes. It then considers the cellular mechanisms of post-injury hyperexcitability and the affective, cognitive, and neurodegenerative changes associated with LFPI. Together, these findings indicate the value of the model while defining the limits of its application to human disease.

papers.title: Novel Genetic Variants of the CHD2 Gene in cis Position in a Patient with Epileptic Encephalopathy: A Case Report and In Silico Analysis of the Impact of the Variants on the Protein.
papers.abstract: CHD2-related neurodevelopmental disorders are increasingly recognized as a distinct group of epileptic encephalopathies with heterogeneous clinical manifestations. Here, we report a 12-year-old female patient with pharmacoresistant epilepsy, mild cognitive impairment (IQ = 56), and extraneurological features including grade II kyphoscoliosis and planovalgus foot deformity. Video-EEG monitoring revealed a phenotype consistent with Jeavons syndrome, characterized by daily eyelid myoclonia with absences and marked photosensitivity with an eye closure sensitivity (ECS) phenomenon. Molecular genetic testing via whole-exome and Sanger sequencing identified two novel variants in the CHD2 gene (NM_001271.4): c.1634T>G (p.Leu545Arg) and c.3810G>C (p.Leu1270Phe). Long-read nanopore sequencing confirmed their de novo status and cis-positioning on the paternal allele. Structural bioinformatic analysis using AlphaFold3, FoldX/mCSM (v5.0 package), UCSF ChimeraX (v1.10.1), and PyMOL (v3.1.8) demonstrated that both variants individually destabilize the CHD2 protein, with a cumulative destabilizing effect when combined: p.Leu545Arg affects the ATP-binding domain, whereas p.Leu1270Phe disrupts hydrophobic packing within the C-terminal DNA-binding domain. These findings suggest accelerated protein degradation as a potential disease mechanism. Our data support the pathogenicity of these heterozygous cis-variants and implicate CHD2 haploinsufficiency as the leading etiopathogenic mechanism, though distinct domain-specific effects of each substitution may also contribute to the complex molecular synergy observed in this case.

papers.title: Temporal Regulation of UVA-Induced Ferroptosis-Associated Injury in Keratinocytes.
papers.abstract: Ferroptosis contributes to ultraviolet (UV)-induced epidermal injury, but whether circadian state modifies keratinocyte susceptibility remains unclear. We integrated human epidermal transcriptomic analyses with functional experiments in HaCaT keratinocytes to compare UVA- and UVB-induced ferroptosis-associated responses and assess their temporal regulation. Both wavelengths reduced cell viability and increased reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and intracellular Fe2+ accumulation; ferrostatin-1 provided partial protection. UVB reduced xCT and GPX4 and showed a proteasome-sensitive component of GPX4 loss, whereas UVA predominantly reduced GPX4 without detectably altering xCT. Human epidermal transcriptomes showed heterogeneous cross-sectional associations among circadian, oxidative-stress, and ferroptosis-related genes, while longitudinal profiles revealed positive temporal coupling between NR1D1-associated signals and GPX4. In synchronized HaCaT cells, ARNTL and NR1D1 displayed 24 h rhythmicity, whereas GPX4 and SLC7A11 did not meet the prespecified rhythmicity criterion. Nevertheless, UVA-induced cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and GPX4 loss varied across post-synchronization time points and were greatest at 24 h. SR8278 partially preserved GPX4 abundance and attenuated UVA-induced loss of viability, reactive oxygen species accumulation, and lipid peroxidation, without significantly affecting Fe2+ accumulation. These findings associate circadian state with temporal variation in UVA-induced ferroptosis susceptibility and implicate the broader clock-redox system rather than rhythmic expression of individual ferroptosis effectors.

papers.title: Seasonal Variation, Circadian Patterns, and Night Eating Syndrome Among Older Adults: The Mediating Role of Sleep Quality.
papers.abstract: Objective: We aimed to examine whether sleep quality mediates the relationship between seasonal variation, circadian pattern, and night eating syndrome in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 336 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥ 60 years) recruited from geriatric social clubs. Participants completed validated instruments, including the Global Seasonality Scale (GSS), Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), Night Eating Diagnostic Questionnaire (NEDQ), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Path analysis with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) was used to estimate direct and indirect associations among the study variables. Results: The mean age was 66.8 ± 5.9 years (56.8% male). Moderate to severe seasonal variation was observed in 68.2% of participants, while 85.1% reported poor sleep quality. Morning circadian pattern predominated (56.9%), and 23.2% met criteria for full night eating syndrome. Path analysis identified a significant indirect association between seasonal variation and circadian pattern through sleep quality (B = -0.038, 95% CI [-0.051, -0.026]), corresponding to 41% of the total modeled association. Similarly, a significant indirect association between seasonal variation and night eating syndrome through sleep quality was observed (B = 0.053, 95% CI [0.037, 0.068]), corresponding to 37% of the total modeled association. All direct and indirect paths were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Sleep quality was significantly involved in the observed relationships between seasonal variation, circadian pattern, and night eating syndrome among older adults, with the path models indicating both direct and indirect associations. These findings emphasize the interconnected nature of seasonal sensitivity, sleep characteristics, circadian preference, and nighttime eating behavior in later life. Further longitudinal research with repeated seasonal assessments is warranted to clarify the temporal relationships among these factors and to determine the potential value of sleep-focused preventive and clinical approaches.

papers.title: Erythrocyte-Associated Proteins Underlie the Reported Oxidative-Stress Enrichment in Plasma Proteomics of Obstructive Sleep Apnoea: A Secondary Quality Marker Analysis of Public Datasets.
papers.abstract: Background: Erythrocyte proteins released into plasma carry oxidation-related annotations and can be read as evidence of oxidative stress. We examined whether this applies to an oxidative-stress enrichment reported in a plasma proteomic study of obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Methods: In a secondary analysis of public data (PXD073409; men; 15 non-OSA, 15 mild OSA, 15 severe OSA; 422 proteins), erythrocyte, platelet and coagulation quality marker indices were computed from the panels of Geyer et al.; the erythrocyte panel was only partly quantified (15 of 29 entries). The original differential and over-representation analyses were repeated with panel members excluded, with adjustment for the erythrocyte index, and with leave-one-protein-out indices. A second public dataset (PXD069503; 15 severe OSA, 15 mild-to-moderate OSA, 15 controls) was used for directional comparison. Clinical covariates were not available. Results: The erythrocyte index was higher in mild (ratio of geometric means 1.74, 95% CI 1.04 to 2.80) and severe OSA (2.43, 1.68 to 3.47) than in non-OSA participants. Six of the 13 proteins that are increased in severe OSA were erythrocyte panel members, and all nine enriched terms consisted of panel members only, including hydrogen peroxide catabolic process (HBA1, HBB, HBD, PRDX2). After adjustment, PRDX2 was accounted for by erythrocyte content, whereas the haemoglobin chains remained elevated and carried seven of the terms. The index alone separated severe- from non-OSA participants (AUROC 0.858); the data could not show whether all 422 proteins (AUROC 0.969) add to it (difference +0.111, 95% CI -0.009 to +0.268). In the second dataset the index was higher in severe OSA than in controls (1.55, 1.06 to 2.35). Conclusions: The reported oxidative-stress enrichment rests on erythrocyte-associated proteins and, on these data, is not evidence of altered oxidative activity in plasma. Whether this content arises before or after venepuncture cannot be determined. Quality marker indices should be reported alongside plasma proteomic biomarker results.

papers.title: Obesity in the 21st Century: Where Do We Stand?
papers.abstract: Obesity in the 21st century has become a global epidemic owing to its heterogeneous aetiology and clinical presentation, as well as the development of associated comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease, type2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, and obesity-related cancers. Notably, cardiovascular disease and diabetes are major contributors to obesity-associated morbidity and mortality. Current diagnostic approaches rely predominantly on anthropometric measurements, which have proven limited in their ability to provide accurate and clinically meaningful stratification of patients with obesity. Consequently, obesity treatments, including metabolic surgery and pharmacological therapies, remain insufficiently tailored to the wide variability in obesity-related genotypes, phenotypes, and endotypes. In this context, a personalised medical approach offers considerable promise. A clear overview of currently effective diagnostic tools and treatments, as well as future possibilities, is therefore needed. Recent developments in precision medicine, multi-omics, biomarkers, and advanced diagnostic technologies may facilitate improved patient stratification and support more individualized therapeutic strategies. Together, these approaches may contribute to a more comprehensive, evidence-based, and patient-centered framework for the prevention, diagnosis, and management of obesity and its complications.

papers.title: Virtual Surgery and CFD in Rhinology: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Background: Nasal obstruction is one of the most common reasons for which patients present to an otolaryngologist, yet the outcomes of operations aimed at improving nasal patency remain inconsistent, and the correlation between conventional objective measures and perceived patency is uncertain. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) allows nasal airflow to be simulated from craniofacial computed tomography; combined with software that reconstructs and modifies sinonasal anatomy, it permits a planned procedure to be reproduced digitally and its functional impact predicted before any tissue is removed. This scoping review maps how CFD-based virtual surgery has been used in rhinology, how the simulations were validated, and which clinical outcomes were reported. Methods: Following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, PubMed and Scopus were searched in October 2025 for studies published between 2015 and 2025. Inclusion criteria restricted papers to English-language studies of virtual surgery tools involving CFD in humans or human-derived models. Pediatric (<18 years), sleep apnea, and orthognathic studies were excluded, as were studies of other parts of the respiratory tract and environmental or toxicological work. Duplicates were removed in Mendeley, and two authors independently screened titles and abstracts. Data were charted by two authors. The review was not registered. Results: Forty-one studies were included, covering the nasal septum, the inferior and middle turbinates, the ostiomeatal complex, the maxillary and sphenoid sinuses, septal perforations, and postoperative synechiae. Virtual results were compared with actual postoperative anatomy, airflow, or symptoms in only 7 of the 41 studies and agreed with them in most respects. In several small studies, a greater extent of resection did not improve airflow further and reduced mucosal heat and moisture exchange, wall shear stress, and regional cooling, but the extent that appeared best depended on the anatomy and the outcome considered. These parameters have been proposed as better correlates of the subjective sense of patency than resistance alone; this has rarely been tested in patients. The most recent work applies machine learning and adjoint optimization as research tools for planning support. Conclusions: CFD-based virtual surgery is a promising tool for planning the extent of rhinological procedures. Its routine use will require standardized methods, prospective validation, and correlation with patient-reported outcomes (NOSE, SNOT-22); larger studies with such endpoints are still lacking.

papers.title: Effects of Occupational Therapy Interventions on Occupational Performance and Physical and Cognitive Fatigue in Adults with Multiple Sclerosis: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) frequently limits participation in daily occupations and is associated with disabling fatigue. However, the effects of occupational therapy (OT) remain uncertain because available trials have evaluated heterogeneous interventions and outcomes. This systematic review synthesized evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on occupational performance and physical and cognitive fatigue in adults with MS. Materials and Methods: Seven bibliographic databases were searched from inception to 10 August 2026: MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) via the Cochrane Library, Web of Science Core Collection, APA PsycINFO via EBSCOhost, CINAHL Complete via EBSCOhost, and ProQuest Central. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using RoB 2. Certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Given the clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively following the Synthesis Without Meta-Analysis guideline. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251115448). Results: Seven RCTs involving 488 randomized participants were included. Findings for occupational performance were inconsistent: one small waitlist-controlled trial reported large short-term benefits from occupational performance coaching, whereas an active-comparator trial found improvements in both groups without clear superiority. Other findings showed no comparative benefit or provided only indirect evidence. Fatigue findings were similarly inconsistent: one 20-participant pilot trial favored a sleep-targeted OT intervention, two trials found no comparative benefit, and one large trial transiently favored usual-care OT. The certainty of evidence was very low for both outcomes.
