This was assessed at baseline and at 1, 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months from baseline. Secondary outcomes included change in anxiety and general health-related quality of life. p-values < 0.050 were considered statistically significant. Two hundred and eleven participants met the inclusion criteria. Over half (n = 126; 59.72%) were users of cannabis at baseline. At the primary endpoint of 24 months, mean SQS improved from 2.46 ± 2.10 (mean ± standard deviation (SD)) at baseline to 5.14 ± 2.75 (mean difference +2.68; 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.23-3.14; p < 0.001), with improvements observed at all timepoints. SQS values of 0 (odds ratio (OR) 15.49; 95% CI 3.87-65.19; p < 0.001) and 1-3 (OR 4.90; 95% CI 1.87-13.80; p = 0.002) at baseline and prescription of dried flower CBMPs (OR 4.99; 95% CI 1.27-21.39; p = 0.025) were associated with clinically significant improvements in sleep quality at 24 months. Seventeen participants (8.06%) reported adverse events. Participants aged over 60 were more likely to report an adverse event (OR 19.08; 95% CI 1.52-535.75; p = 0.036). Initiation of CBMPs was associated with improvements in self-reported sleep quality across 2 years, with the largest associations observed in those with the most severe impairment. As an uncontrolled, observational study of a self-selected and predominantly cannabis-experienced cohort, placebo effects, regression to the mean, and selection bias cannot be excluded.

papers.title: Multidomain Polysomnographic Abnormalities in Cervical Dystonia: REM Suppression, Respiratory Instability, and Sensorimotor Dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Cervical dystonia (CD) is considered a basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical and brainstem network disorder rather than an isolated focal motor disease. Our aim was to analyze sleep architecture, REM physiology, respiratory patterns, and sensorimotor activity in CD using full-night PSG. We conducted a full-night PSG case-control analysis involving 33 CD patients and 20 matched controls. Clinical scales used were Toronto Western Spasmodic Torticollis Rating Scale (TWSTRS), Craniocervical Dystonia Questionnaire (CDQ-24), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI), and Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS). CD patients showed greater sleep disruption than controls with significantly decreased total sleep time (TST) and reduced sleep efficiency (SE). Wake after sleep onset (WASO) was considerably higher. >70% met criteria for a study-defined severe insomnia pattern (<25% of controls). REM was absent in 42% of patients and overall REM percentage was reduced by ~70%. CD showed nearly three-fold higher apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), a significantly higher obstructive apnea index, and prolonged respiratory event duration. Periodic limb movements (PLMS) index was ~14 times higher. Spontaneous arousal rates were significantly increased. Greater motor disability (TWSTRS) correlated with decreased N3 sleep. Higher Tsui severity correlated with increased N2 sleep, linking clinical severity to altered sleep architecture. BDI correlated with higher AHI, greater respiratory event burden and obstructive apnea index. PLMS index showed strong internal coupling with PLMS arousal index and correlated with cardiac parameters. Sleep measures may offer a useful non-invasive perspective on distributed network features associated with CD. These findings are associative and require replication in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Atopic dermatitis.
papers.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease that commonly begins in childhood and can persist or first appear in adulthood. Its burden reflects pruritus, sleep loss, pain, infection, psychosocial effects, and treatment demands rather than visible extent alone. Diagnosis is clinical and requires recognition of age- and skin tone-specific morphology and exclusion of mimics. AD management begins with moisturization, gentle bathing, topical anti-inflammatory therapy, education, and proactive maintenance. Newer nonsteroidal topical agents and targeted systemic therapies have expanded options, but treatment should be individualized according to age, disease severity and control, comorbidities, safety, access, and patient preference. Routine elimination diets, topical antimicrobials for uninfected disease, antihistamines as primary antipruritic therapy, and systemic corticosteroids are generally not recommended for AD. This review provides physician associates with a practical approach to diagnosis, severity assessment, stepwise treatment, complication recognition, and timely referral.
papers.journal: JAAPA : official journal of the American Academy of Physician Assistants

papers.title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Sleep and Socioeconomic Status Among Cancer Survivors in the United States.
papers.abstract: Sleep problems are common among cancer survivors and are linked to poorer quality of life. In the general United States (US) population, socioeconomic status (SES) is strongly associated with sleep health, but emerging evidence suggests that these benefits may be diminished among non-White racial/ethnic groups. Whether such patterns extend to cancer survivors is unknown. We analyzed data on 25,732 adult cancer survivors from National Health Interview Surveys. Sleep duration (normal 6-8 h; short ≤ 5 h; long ≥ 9 h) and troubled sleep (≥ 3 days/week of difficulty falling or staying asleep) were assessed via self-report. SES indicators included educational attainment and family income. Poisson regression models with race/ethnicity-by-SES interaction terms were used to estimate racial/ethnic differences in SES-sleep associations. Among non-Hispanic (NH) White survivors, higher education and income were consistently associated with lower prevalence of short sleep and troubled sleep. These SES gradients were muted or reversed among NH Black and Hispanic survivors. For example, NH White survivors with a bachelor's degree had substantially lower odds of short sleep compared with those with ≤ high school education, whereas no such association was observed among NH Black or Hispanic survivors. When stratifying by both education and income, income showed more consistent associations with sleep across all groups, while additional benefits of higher education were observed only among NH White survivors. SES-sleep gradients differ markedly across racial/ethnic groups among US cancer survivors. Tailored interventions addressing structural and socioeconomic inequities may be needed to improve sleep health and reduce disparities in survivorship.

papers.title: Human Engineered Heart Tissues Reproduce Trigger- and Substrate-Driven Mechanisms of Ventricular Tachycardia.
papers.abstract: Human iPSC‑derived engineered heart tissues (EHTs) are used to model cardiac physiology and drug responses, yet whether they reproduce tissue‑scale ventricular arrhythmia mechanisms remains unclear. We combined modified milliPillar EHT fabrication with high-resolution dual-channel voltage/Ca2+ optical mapping. Baseline electrophysiology showed action potential durations (APD) within the range reported for human ventricles and conduction velocities approximately half of human longitudinal values, with rate‑dependent restitution of APD and Ca2+ transient duration, conduction slowing, and physiologic AP-Ca2+ latency. To interrogate a trigger arm of ventricular tachycardia (VT), we modeled acquired long-QT syndrome (aLQTS; hERG blockade with hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia) in EHTs from two hiPSC lines. aLQTS EHTs developed VT-like episodes with beat‑to‑beat instability. Early afterdepolarizations propagated heterogeneously, generating triggered activity, tissue acceleration, APD dispersion, wavebreak, and rotor formation. These were short and self-terminating (median 0.4 s) and clustered at head/neck region curvatures. To test whether a fixed spatial substrate supports prolonged reentry, we developed a reproducible focal cryoinjury model. After injury, all tissues developed VT-like episodes, and 70% anatomically anchored rotors at the border; three persisted beyond 10 s, a recording-limited lower bound. Dual voltage/Ca2+ mapping at this resolution establishes EHTs as a non-animal platform for mechanistic study of both trigger- and substrate-driven ventricular arrhythmias.

papers.title: A neuropsychiatric presentation of suspected immune-mediatedneuropathy: diagnostic overlap between Guillain-Barré syndrome andautoimmune encephalitis-a case.
papers.abstract: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy classically characterized by rapidly progressive, symmetrical limb weakness and areflexia. Although neuropsychiatric manifestations have been described, they remain uncommon and may lead to diagnostic delay or misattribution to primary psychiatric illness. We describe a 58-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis who presented with hematemesis secondary to gastritis and altered mental status (AMS), preceded by several weeks of progressive behavioral changes, including withdrawal, dysphoria, hallucinations, and disorientation. During hospitalization, her mental status continued to decline despite trials of antipsychotic and benzodiazepine therapy. Neurological examination revealed progressive ascending weakness, areflexia, and sensory deficits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated albuminocytologic dissociation. In the absence of electrophysiological confirmation, the findings raised concern for an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy such as Guillain-Barré syndrome; however, definitive classification was not possible because electrophysiological testing was not performed. The patient was treated with a five-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), after which both motor function and mental status improved; however, treatment response was interpreted cautiously because IVIG is not disease-specific. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of neuropsychiatric presentations in suspected GBS. The prominence and early onset of psychiatric symptoms necessitated a broad differential diagnosis, including delirium, metabolic encephalopathy, autoimmune encephalitis, and acute porphyria. Additionally, the patient's history of rheumatoid arthritis raised consideration of alternative immune-mediated neuropathies, including vasculitic neuropathy. Importantly, autoimmune encephalitis could not be excluded due to the absence of neuroimaging, EEG, and antibody testing. Furthermore, clinical improvement following IVIG is not disease-specific and may occur in multiple autoimmune conditions. This case underscores the diagnostic tension between peripheral and central nervous system autoimmune processes in the setting of incomplete diagnostic data. GBS should remain a consideration in patients presenting with concurrent neurological and psychiatric symptoms; however, caution is warranted when diagnostic studies are limited. This case emphasizes the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis and highlights the potential for overlap between peripheral neuropathies and central autoimmune encephalopathies. Early multidisciplinary evaluation and careful interpretation of treatment response are essential for optimizing patient outcomes. This report should be interpreted as an educational case illustrating the diagnostic complexity of overlapping neuropsychiatric and peripheral neurological manifestations rather than as definitive evidence of an atypical presentation of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

papers.title: Multi-omics analysis reveals that sleep deprivation exacerbates intestinal barrier injury via the microbiota-dependent taurodeoxycholic acid/group 3 innate lymphoid/IL-22 axis.
papers.abstract: Clinical studies demonstrated a correlation between sleep dysfunction and intestinal diseases. However, the detailed interactions and underlying mechanisms linking sleep disruption to intestinal microenvironment remain poorly understood. We employed the Curling Prevention by Water (CPW) paradigm to establish a mouse model of sleep deprivation (SD) for durations ranging from 0 to 96 h. The dynamic changes in the intestinal microenvironment were systematically profiled using multi-omics approaches, including metagenomic sequencing, untargeted metabolomics and RNA sequencing. The causal role of microbial dysbiosis and the underlying mechanisms were further investigated using germ-free mice, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), flow cytometry, and targeted intervention. The intestinal microenvironment was highly sensitive to SD. Distinct microbial communities and metabolite profiles were observed among brief SD (< 24 h of SD), prolonged SD (24-96 h of SD) and control. Brief SD triggered a self-regulatory response of the gut microbiota, characterized by an increase in certain beneficial bacteria (e.g., Parabacteroides goldsteinii). In contrast, prolonged SD shaped a pro-inflammatory microbial structure, characterized by reduced Akkermansia muciniphila and enriched Pseudomonadota. Multi-omics analysis revealed that SD significantly inhibited microbial bile acid metabolism, particularly taurodeoxycholic acid (TDCA), and impaired intestinal barrier function while suppressing the intestinal immune response to bacteria antigens. Mechanistically, SD exacerbated intestinal barrier damage by inhibiting the TDCA/group 3 innate lymphoid cells (ILC3)/IL-22 axis. Supplementation with TDCA effectively restored ILC3 function, IL-22 production, and barrier integrity in SD mice. Furthermore, FMT from patients with sleep dysfunction significantly disturbed intestinal microenvironment and increased serum cortisol by regulating gut microbiota and inhibiting TDCA/ILC3/IL-22 axis. This study dynamically delineates how SD disrupts intestinal homeostasis by reshaping the gut microbiota and suppressing the TDCA/ILC3/IL-22 axis. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights and identify potential therapeutic targets for sleep dysfunction-associated intestinal complications.

papers.title: Compartment-specific cAMP dysfunction in diabetic cardiomyopathy in hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes: therapeutic potential of fibroblast growth factor 1.
papers.abstract: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) represents a distinct form of heart failure occurring independently of coronary artery disease, yet effective treatments remain limited. While cAMP signaling alterations have been reported in diabetic hearts, the compartment-specific consequences across distinct subcellular pools remain poorly understood. We investigated cytosolic and mitochondrial cAMP microdomain dysfunction in DCM, focusing on ADCY2 and PDE4DIP as potential regulators, and evaluated fibroblast growth factor 1 (FGF1) as a therapeutic intervention using integrated two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived cardiac models. Healthy hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes were exposed to a diabetic-like environment (high glucose, endothelin-1 and cortisol) in 2D and 3D culture. Two-dimensional studies included bulk RNA sequencing, FRET-based cAMP measurements in cytosolic and mitochondrial outer membrane compartments, and microelectrode array electrophysiology. Three-dimensional cardiac microtissues were assessed by optical mapping to characterize spatial calcium dynamics and conduction properties. DCM exhibited compartment-specific cAMP dysregulation associated with ADCY2 downregulation and PDE4DIP upregulation. Cytosolic compartments showed preserved baseline cAMP but attenuated forskolin responsiveness, while the mitochondrial outer membrane displayed both reduced baseline cAMP and impaired stimulated responses. Transcriptomic analysis revealed transcriptional signatures consistent with metabolic remodeling, including upregulated fatty acid oxidation machinery, Complex I dysfunction, and elevated phospholamban and CASQ2 expression. 3D optical mapping demonstrated reduced calcium transient amplitude, prolonged transient duration, and severely impaired calcium propagation velocity. FGF1 treatment normalized PDE4DIP expression and restored cAMP dynamics in 2D cultures and partially improved calcium transient amplitude in 3D microtissues, though conduction defects persisted. Compartment-specific impairment of cAMP microdomains is associated with DCM pathogenesis. Integrated 2D-3D assessment reveals that FGF1 improves cAMP signaling but does not fully reverse metabolic, electrophysiological, or structural abnormalities, highlighting the need for combination therapies targeting both cAMP pathway integrity and conduction restoration.

papers.title: The importance of body fat percentage: associations between fatigue, sleep, body composition, and perceived physical activity barriers in young women.
papers.abstract: Physical inactivity is highly prevalent among young women and is shaped by interacting biological and psychophysiological factors. Although fatigue and sleep disturbances have been associated with perceived physical activity barriers, the role of physiological indicators, particularly body composition, remains insufficiently clarified. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the associations between body composition, fatigue, sleep quality, and perceived physical activity barriers in young women. A total of 392 female university students (aged 19-24 years) participated in the study. The mean body fat percentage was 28.18 ± 7.79, and the mean personal barrier score was 2.41 ± 0.70. Fatigue, sleep quality, and perceived physical activity barriers were assessed using validated scales, and body composition was measured via bioelectrical impedance analysis. Correlation and hierarchical regression analyses were conducted. Body fat percentage and physical fatigue were positively associated with perceived physical activity barriers, with stronger associations observed for personal barriers (r = .35 and r = .32, respectively). Sleep-related variables showed weaker and less consistent associations across barrier dimensions (r values ranged from 0.12 to 0.26). In regression models, body fat percentage showed the strongest and most consistent association with perceived physical activity barriers (β values ranged from 0.24 to 0.28), followed by physical fatigue (β values ranged from 0.12 to 0.22), whereas sleep-onset difficulties demonstrated smaller and less stable associations (β values ranged from 0.11 to 0.15). The overall explained variance was limited (R² values ranged from 0.09 to 0.18). Perceived physical activity barriers among young women were associated with body fat percentage, fatigue, and sleep-related difficulties, with body fat percentage emerging as the most consistent physiological correlate. Physical fatigue demonstrated stronger and more consistent associations with perceived barriers than sleep-related variables. These findings should be interpreted as associative rather than causal because of the cross-sectional design and highlight the importance of considering both physiological and psychophysiological factors when examining perceived barriers to physical activity.

papers.title: The effect of an eye mask-based blackout protocol on patients' sleep quality and melatonin levels: a randomised controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is among the most common problems in intensive care units due to continuous lighting, noise, and ongoing medical interventions. Disturbed circadian rhythms may decrease melatonin secretion and adversely affect patient recovery and well-being. Creating a dark environment during sleep may improve sleep quality and support melatonin regulation. To evaluate the effect of an eye mask-based blackout protocol on sleep quality and melatonin levels in patients hospitalised in the chest intensive care unit. This randomised controlled trial was conducted in the chest intensive care unit of a university hospital between August 2024 and May 2025. Sixty patients were randomly assigned to experimental (n = 30) and control (n = 30) groups. The experimental group received an eye mask-based blackout protocol (eye mask from 11:00 p.m. to 05:00 a.m. with a standardised nighttime light-reduction procedure), while the control group received routine care. Urine samples were collected overnight to measure melatonin metabolite (aMT6s) levels, and data were obtained using the Sleep Quality Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Richard Campbell Sleep Scale. Pre- and post-test values were compared and analysed using appropriate statistical tests. Sleep quality scores and urinary aMT6s levels were significantly higher in the experimental group after the intervention (p < 0.001). The mean VAS score rose from 4.33 to 7.97, and the Richard Campbell Sleep Scale score increased from 224.67 to 447.50. Urinary aMT6s (ng/mg creatinine) increased from 15.06 to 97.09. No significant improvements in subjective sleep quality were observed in the control group, although urinary aMT6s levels also increased, suggesting that factors other than the intervention may have influenced aMT6s values. An eye mask-based blackout protocol may improve sleep quality and may be associated with increased urinary aMT6s levels in intensive care patients. Eye mask use is a simple, inexpensive, and non-invasive nursing intervention that may enhance patient comfort and improve subjective sleep quality in intensive care settings. This clinical trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov with the identifier NCT07385768 (Record name/ID: ATAUNI-SLEEP-ICU-01). The record was initially released on 20 January 2026 and was last publicly released on 29 January 2026.

papers.title: Exploration of shift work among nursing professionals related to interconnected determinants of health in a hospital: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: To explore sleep quality and its co-occurrence with interconnected health variables (perceived stress, general mental health, everyday memory complaints, and quality of life) among nursing professionals, evaluating differences across shift work, gender, and age subgroups. A cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted at Son Espases University Hospital (Spain). Data were collected between March 3 and March 24, 2025, using an online questionnaire distributed via corporate email. A total of 247 nursing professionals (85.8% female, aged 21-65) completed standardized tools: PSQI (sleep quality), MCTQ (chronotype), PSS-14 (perceived stress), GHQ-12 (general mental health), MFE-30 (memory failures), and WHOQOL-BREF (quality of life). Across all shifts, participants exhibited poor sleep quality (PSQI > 5), a high prevalence of undefined chronotype (64-66%), moderate stress (~ 26 points), psychological distress (~ 14 points), and memory complaints (~ 58 points), while maintaining favorable quality of life (~ 90 points). Day-shift workers reported significantly higher sleep medication use than rotating-shift workers (p = .011). Subgroup analyses revealed that females on rotating shifts reported significantly more memory complaints than males (p = .005), and professionals over 50 years on fixed night shifts presented significantly poorer mental health (p = .024) and severe memory complaints (p = .012). Nursing professionals present widespread poor sleep quality, moderate stress, and subjective cognitive complaints, with greater mental health and memory vulnerability observed among females on rotating shifts and workers aged over 50 on night shifts. Rather than generic measures, organizational strategies should implement tailored shift scheduling aligned with individual chronotypes and age, integrate routine occupational monitoring of sleep and mental health, and provide targeted stress-management interventions.

papers.title: Association between built environment and sleep duration mediated by air pollution: a cohort study in China.
papers.abstract: The joint effects of complex built environment exposures on sleep duration and their underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the overall effects of residential built environment mixtures on longitudinal changes in sleep duration, and to explore potential mediation through air pollution. We analyzed data from 18,891 adults in Yinzhou cohort in China, with baseline (2015-2017) and follow-up (2021-2023) assessments. Sleep duration was self-reported via questionnaires. Linear mixed models and quantile g-computation were employed to evaluate the associations between built environment mixture (green and blue space, light at night [LAN], walkability, road proximity, and population density) and longitudinal change of sleep duration. Structural equation modeling was utilized to assess mediation by air pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, and NO2). Each quartile increase in the built environment mixture index was associated with a 0.057 h/year (95%CI: 0.039, 0.075) increase in sleep duration. Walkability (37.4%), green space (28.4%), and blue space (26.5%) drove the protective effects, whereas population density (63.3%) and LAN (36.7%) contributed negatively. Furthermore, interquartile range (IQR) increases in PM10, PM2.5, and NO2 were significantly associated with shorter sleep duration (β=-0.027 h, -0.048 h, and - 0.071 h, respectively). Air pollutants partially mediated the associations, with mediation proportions varying across exposures; notably, lower NO2 and PM2.5 explained up to 45.3% and 21.5% of the protective effects of walkability and green space on sleep duration, respectively. Built environment features were significantly associated with sleep duration changes, partially through air pollution. Optimizing urban planning while mitigating air pollution may support sleep health.

papers.title: Characterizing and conceptualizing sleep in adolescents and young adults with cystic fibrosis: a descriptive qualitative study.
papers.abstract: The adolescent and young adult (AYA) developmental period is a time of risk for sleep challenges. These may be additionally compounded for those living with cystic fibrosis (CF). This study aimed to better understand how AYA with CF describe and experience sleep. Purposive sampling, from within a larger quantitative study of AYA with CF aged 14-25, aimed for maximum variation in sleep experiences as defined by score on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Virtual, semi-structured interviews were conducted. Open-ended questions focussed on sleep experience and factors perceived to be associated with both a good and poor night's sleep. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed and de-identified. Data were analyzed independently by two researchers using content analysis and following qualitative descriptive methodology. Codes were categorized into overarching, mutually exclusive themes. Interviews were conducted with 19 participants (mean age = 19.74 ± 3.19yrs). As determined by the PSQI, 42% (n = 8) had poor sleep quality. CF symptoms, CF treatments, anxiety, changes in health status, and initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ ivacaftor (ETI) were perceived to interfere with sleep. Positioning, good sleep hygiene, breathing therapies and being stable on ETI were perceived to benefit sleep. AYA's with CF discussed a desire to engage in discussions about sleep with their CF care teams. Given the prevalence of sleep concerns, sleep assessment and screening should be prioritized in CF care. Identifying sleep challenges and better understanding the factors that contribute towards or ameliorate poor sleep could have a significant impact on well-being and quality of life.

papers.title: FT-IR-based strategy for Streptococcus pneumoniae serotyping using machine-learning classifiers.
papers.abstract: Rapid serotype identification of circulating Streptococcus pneumoniae is essential for both effective epidemiological surveillance and clinical management. The gold standard serotyping method (Quellung reaction) is time-consuming, labor-intensive and expensive. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy using the IR-Biotyper® (Bruker Daltonics GmbH, Bremen, Germany) system has recently been proposed as a rapid and low-cost technique for serotype identification, based on spectral analysis of capsular polysaccharide components. The integration of machine learning algorithms within the IR-Biotyper® enables automated analysis and classification of FT-IR spectra, allowing rapid prediction of pneumococcal serotypes. The present study evaluated the application of machine learning algorithms for serotype identification in clinical S. pneumoniae isolates using the IR-Biotyper® system. A database with 128 isolates, representing 30 different serotypes, was used to develop four classifiers. A global classifier was designed to predict twelve serotypes (3, 4, 6A/6C, 7C/7F, 12F, 15A/15B/15C, 19A/19F, 22F, 23A/23B/23F, 24B/24F, 35B and 38) achieving 99% accuracy. Additionally, three sequential sub-classifiers were developed to differentiate; 6A from 6C, 15A from 15B and 15C, and 23A from 23B and 23F, with validation dataset accuracies of 100%, 89% and 100% respectively. The evaluation of unknown serotypes showed 92% accuracy. FT-IR spectroscopy showed high concordance with Quellung reaction, supporting its use as a rapid and cost-effective method for serotype identification of S. pneumoniae. Sequential sub-classification represents a practical strategy that could be used to classify additional serotypes of epidemiological relevance.

papers.title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

papers.title: Attenuated PER3 amplitude in hair follicles is associated with sleep irregularity in schizophrenia.
papers.abstract: Circadian dysregulation is prevalent in both schizophrenia and obesity, yet the molecular mechanisms underpinning these disturbances remain unclear. We examined circadian variation in clock gene expression using repeated hair follicle self-sampling across two days in 66 adults: 22 with schizophrenia and obesity (SCH-OB), 22 with obesity but no psychiatric disorder (OB), and 22 normal-weight controls (LEAN). Gene expression was quantified by qPCR, and complementary markers included salivary cortisol and melatonin, oral pH and temperature, and accelerometer-derived sleep metrics. Evidence of rhythmic expression was detected in five of six clock genes. PER3 amplitude was significantly reduced in SCH-OB compared with both OB and LEAN (p < 0.01) and correlated positively with sleep regularity (p = 0.006). Cortisol rhythms were preserved across groups, whereas melatonin amplitude was attenuated in SCH-OB relative to LEAN (p < 0.05). Hair follicle sampling proved highly feasible, with >98% compliance. These findings indicate that individuals with schizophrenia exhibit dampened circadian rhythms in PER3 expression that parallel irregular sleep patterns, supporting hair follicle-based sampling as a practical tool for assessing molecular rhythm parameters in real-world conditions.

papers.title: [Mechanisms and outcome evaluation of neurofeedback in post-traumatic stress disorder intervention].
papers.abstract: Patients with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) still face challenges such as limited treatment response in some cases and substantial inter-individual variability when receiving existing interventions. Neurofeedback (NFB), as a closed-loop neuromodulation approach based on brain-computer interface (BCI), can guide patients to regulate abnormal neural activity patterns by providing real-time feedback on brain activity features, and therefore shows potential for PTSD rehabilitation. This paper reviews the regulatory mechanisms of NFB on the prefrontal-limbic emotion regulation circuit and the dysregulated states of the default mode network, salience network, and central executive network. It compares three major modalities, including electroencephalography, real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy, in terms of feedback targets, spatiotemporal resolution, and clinical applicability. Based on a multidimensional evaluation framework composed of clinical scales, neurophysiological indicators, and functional recovery indicators, this paper further discusses the clinical positioning of NFB relative to first-line treatments and the potential synergistic mechanisms of its combined application with psychological interventions. Current studies still face limitations such as insufficient control design and a lack of standardized training parameters. Future research should integrate individualized target selection and machine learning-based modeling to promote the standardized application of NFB.

papers.title: [Multi-scale motor imagery electroencephalogram classification framework with dynamic weighted multi-source domain alignment].
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology facilitates information exchange between the brain and external devices, offering new approaches to human-computer interaction and medical rehabilitation. However, distribution shifts caused by inter-subject variability in electroencephalogram (EEG) signals limit classification performance and generalization. To address this issue, DWDANet, an EEG classification framework integrating multi-scale spatiotemporal feature modeling with dynamically weighted domain alignment, is developed. Multi-scale convolutions extracted spatiotemporal features, while a Transformer encoder modeled global dependencies. Multi-source domain alignment with dynamic weighting enhanced collaborative modeling across source domains and improved generalization. In within-subject evaluations, DWDANet achieved accuracies of 87.22%, 90.32%, and 68.82% on the BCI IV-2a, BCI IV-2b, and SHU-MI datasets, respectively. In cross-subject experiments, it achieved accuracies of 70.61%, 81.43%, and 64.38% on these datasets, respectively, outperforming other existing methods on all three. These results indicate that DWDANet could provide an effective approach to improving motor imagery EEG classification performance and cross-subject generalization.

papers.title: [Interpretable dynamic adjacency graph attention network for epileptic seizure detection].
papers.abstract: To address the insufficient robustness of existing deep learning methods in modeling cross-channel dependencies in epileptic electroencephalogram (EEG) signals and the limited traceability of their decision-making rationale, this paper proposes an interpretable dynamic adjacency graph attention network (DA-GAT). The proposed model first extracts EEG features through a convolutional module, and subsequently introduces a dynamic graph learning module and a multi-head graph attention module with prior-gated fusion to achieve automatic epileptic EEG detection. Experimental results on three public datasets, namely the Children's Hospital Boston-Massachusetts Institute of Technology (CHB-MIT), Helsinki, and Siena datasets, demonstrate that DA-GAT outperforms the selected comparison methods in terms of accuracy, F1-score, and other evaluation metrics. Furthermore, by combining gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) with dynamic adjacency matrix visualization, DA-GAT provides interpretable evidence to support clinical review. In summary, this study provides a new methodological approach to cross-channel dependency modeling and interpretability analysis of epileptic EEG signals, and provides a reference for improving the reliability and clinical applicability of deep learning models for automatic epilepsy detection.

papers.title: [A covariance matrix correction method for effective sample size mismatch in event-related potential].
papers.abstract: Covariance matrix estimation is a fundamental problem in event-related potential (ERP) signal processing. Conventional methods systematically overestimate the effective sample size due to temporal autocorrelation and nonstationarity in ERP data. This overestimation degrades the accuracy of covariance matrix estimation, thereby compromising the performance and stability of downstream tasks such as blind source separation and brain decoding. To address this problem, we propose an autocorrelation-corrected Ledoit-Wolf method (AC-LW), which estimates a variance inflation factor from pooled channel-wise lag-one autocorrelations and applies a bounded correction to the Ledoit-Wolf estimator. In controlled tests with strong temporal autocorrelation and nonstationary residuals, AC-LW reduced the squared Frobenius error by 79.47% compared with empirical covariance estimation and by 17.40% compared with the best-performing baseline, the Bartz-Müller method. In typical downstream task evaluations involving ERP components such as N400 and P300, the improved covariance estimation quality brought significant classification performance gains to spatial filter-based single-trial decoding. Overall, AC-LW provides a lightweight and robust correction for electroencephalography spatial covariance matrix estimation.

papers.title: Why does restless legs syndrome emerge in Parkinson's disease? A state-dependent sensorimotor gating reserve hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) occurs in Parkinson's disease (PD), but its interpretation is complicated by nocturnal off-period discomfort, painful dystonia, akathisia, and leg motor restlessness. We ask whether PD creates a distinct mechanism or lowers the threshold for shared idiopathic-RLS biology. Dopamine may modify this threshold alongside rest, nocturnal state, and movement-related sensory processing. Integrating evidence on iron dyshomeostasis, adenosine-glutamate regulation, thalamo-sensorimotor networks, and sleep-circadian state, we propose sensorimotor gating reserve as an integrative framework for the capacity to prevent low-priority leg signals from engaging action systems. PD may reduce this reserve; RLS susceptibility and nocturnal rest may then cross the symptom threshold, while movement temporarily restores separation. Direct PD-RLS evidence remains limited; the model is a testable hypothesis for a phenotypically defined subset. Three comparisons examine within-patient transitions across asymptomatic rest, symptomatic nocturnal rest, and movement-induced relief, with idiopathic RLS and RLS mimics in PD as controls.

papers.title: Stepwise clinical and composite risk score model for predicting obesity hypoventilation syndrome in patients with obesity and sleep-disordered breathing.
papers.abstract: To identify factors associated with obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) and to develop and internally validate a stepwise clinical model and composite risk score in patients with obesity and sleep-disordered breathing. This retrospective cross-sectional study included 213 patients with obesity (body mass index ≥30 kg/m²) who underwent type I polysomnography (PSG) and arterial blood gas (ABG) testing. OHS was defined as a daytime PaCO₂ ≥ 45 mmHg. A three-tier stepwise model was constructed: step 1-clinical factors (male sex, Epworth Sleepiness Scale [ESS] score ≥16, awake SpO₂ <92%); step 2-polysomnography severity (apnea-hypopnea index ≥60/h, minimum SpO₂ <70%, or T90 ≥ 20%); and step 3-biochemical parameter (serum bicarbonate [HCO₃-] ≥27 mmol/L). A composite risk score was derived from multivariate logistic regression and evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Independent predictors of OHS includes male sex, ESS ≥ 16, and serum HCO3- ≥ 27 mmol/L. The stepwise algorithm demonstrated increasing specificity across tiers, reaching 99% specificity and a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of 18.10 when all three steps were positive. The composite risk score (range: 0-12) exhibited good discrimination and stratified patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk categories (OHS prevalence rates: 6.2%, 26.1%, and 61.9%, respectively). A high-risk cutoff score ≥ 7 points yielded 95% specificity, 62% positive predictive value, and LR+ 5.88 for identifying OHS. The proposed three-step model and composite risk score provide a noninvasive tool for identifying OHS in patients with obesity. This approach facilitates targeted ABG testing and early intervention, particularly in resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Intensive Care Unit Delirium in Critically Ill Adults: Evidence-Based Approaches to Prevention and Management.
papers.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 80% of critically ill adults and is associated with increased mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and long-term cognitive decline. Despite strong evidence supporting strategies for delirium management, adherence to best practices is inconsistent, and traditional practices often override their implementation. This clinical review highlights opportunities for deimplementation of outdated practices and adoption of evidence-based strategies to detect, prevent, and manage ICU delirium. Emphasis is placed on validated screening tools, light sedation practices, sleep promotion, and multicomponent care bundles. Empowering nurses with knowledge, autonomy, and interdisciplinary collaboration is essential to improving delirium-related outcomes.
papers.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America

papers.title: Domain-Specific Oral Hypofunction in Older Adults With Obstructive Sleep Apnoea: A Case-Control Study.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) has been associated with dysphagia and tongue muscle dysfunction, but its relationship with multidimensional oral hypofunction remains unclear. This study examined whether polysomnography-confirmed OSA is associated with domain-specific oral hypofunction in older adults. In this case-control study, adults aged ≥ 50 years were included. OSA was defined as an apnoea-hypopnea index ≥ 5 events/h, while controls were defined as having low OSA risk (STOP-Bang < 3). Oral hypofunction was assessed across seven domains. Sex-stratified analyses and multivariable logistic regression models were performed. A total of 288 participants were included (OSA: n = 69; controls: n = 219). Compared with controls, participants with OSA demonstrated poorer oral hygiene (p < 0.001), greater oral dryness (p = 0.005) and lower tongue pressure (p = 0.022). In contrast, declines in occlusal force and chewing function were more prevalent in controls. Adjusted analyses showed that OSA was independently associated with oral hypofunction (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.49, 95% CI: 1.07-5.81), poor oral hygiene (aOR = 4.02), oral dryness (aOR = 4.24) and reduced tongue pressure (aOR = 4.95). Similar oral environmental impairments were observed across both sexes, while tongue pressure reduction was more pronounced in males. OSA is associated with impaired oral environment and reduced tongue pressure. These findings suggest that oral function assessment, particularly tongue pressure measurement, may complement the clinical evaluation of older adults with OSA and help identify individuals at increased risk of swallowing impairment. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05977296.

papers.title: Neurocognitive characteristics of perceptual feedback processing differ in autism.
papers.abstract: Autistic individuals often show reduced adaptation to changing environmental demands, but the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We asked whether it may be explained by reduced sensitivity to external feedback and changes in task difficulty. Autistic and non-autistic adults of either sex, matched for cognitive ability, performed a pitch discrimination task in which their response was immediately followed by feedback. Accuracy was similar between the two groups, yet autistic participants exhibited a markedly reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an event-related EEG potential differentiating explicit negative versus positive feedback. They also showed weaker modulation of feedback-evoked EEG responses by perceptual difficulty. Lastly, they showed reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up experiment conducted 1-2 years later. When combined they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with about 80% accuracy. Together, our findings indicate that multiple processes for evaluating perceptual decisions and adjusting subsequent behavior differ in autism and likely contribute to slow updating in changing contexts.Significance Statement Autism is associated with reduced adaptation to changing environments in both behavior and neural signals, but the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that autistic individuals exhibit a reduced feedback-related negativity (FRN), an EEG component that is present when receiving negative instead of positive feedback. They also show weaker neural modulation by perceptual difficulty and reduced trial-by-trial behavioral updating of perceptual bias following recent correct and easy trials. These effects were replicated in a follow-up study. When combined, they classified autistic and non-autistic participants with high accuracy. These findings suggest that reduced flexibility in autism is associated with reduced processing of external feedback and task difficulty.
