Hypoxic burden, systemic inflammation and respiratory muscle dysfunction in obstructive sleep apnoea: a multicentre cross-sectional study.
Home video sleep recording as a predictor of polysomnography-diagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea in a developmentally normal paediatric population.
Circadian aging and neurodegeneration: the emerging role of the melatonin-cortisol axis in brain homeostasis, disease progression, and precision chronomedicine.
papers.abstract: Circadian aging may promote neurodegenerative illnesses by dysregulating the melatonin-cortisol axis. Low nighttime melatonin synthesis, blunted cortisol circadian cycles, abnormal clock-gene oscillation patterns, and sleep-wake architecture undermine central and peripheral circadian equilibrium with age. Neuroendocrine alterations produce oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, pervasive neuroinflammation (CNS immune function loss), and proteostasis. Increasing Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, Huntington's, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body disease, PTSD, and vascular cognitive impairment due to impaired glymphatic axonal clearance/blood-brain barrier dysregulation/synaptic degeneration/pathoproteopathic protein We examine how clock genes, melatonin signaling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis administration, microglia reactivity, and immune-mediated metabolic dysregulation affect dementia. New endocrine, transcriptomic, multi-omics, and wearable-derived digital biomarkers, chronopharmacology (including melatonin receptor agonists), bright-light therapy, time-restricted eating with exercise chronotherapy guidance/synchronization, sleep optimization, and gut microbiota modulation This study addressed inter-individual circadian variability, genetic susceptibility to therapy timing, biomarker standardization, and clinical trial design. The melatonin-cortisol axis may identify and treat age-related neurodegenerative diseases with tailored treatment.

papers.title: Sleep and Sedentary Behavior Predict Severity in MASLD but Not MetALD/ALD: A Compositional Analysis.
papers.abstract: Daily movement behaviors are typically analyzed in isolation, ignoring their inherent competition for time within the 24-hour day. We examined whether the 24-hour composition of sleep, sedentary time, and physical activity was associated with liver stiffness in adults with steatotic liver disease (SLD) METHOD: This cross-sectional analysis used NHANES 2017-2018 data from 1,080 adults with SLD (889 MASLD, 101MetALD, and 90 ALD). Sleep, sedentary time, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and other waking activity were modelled using isometric log-ratio coordinates in survey-weighted regression with log-transformed liver stiffness measurement (LSM). Isotemporal substitution analyses estimated LSM changes from reallocating 30 minutes between behaviors. In MASLD, a greater sedentary time relative to active behaviors was associated with 5.79% higher LSM (95% CI 1.14-10.66%; p=0.027) after sociodemographic adjustment, attenuating after cardiometabolic adjustment (3.73%; p=0.086). Greater sleep relative to all other behaviors was independently associated with 15.55% lower LSM (95% CI -27.33% to -1.86%; p=0.044), persisting after full adjustment (-14.38%, 95% CI -25.58% to -1.49%; p=0.047). Replacing 30 minutes of sedentary time with sleep was associated with a larger LSM reduction (-1.69%, 95% CI -2.98% to -0.39%; p=0.011) than replacement with MVPA (-0.83%, 95% CI -1.32% to -0.33%; p=0.001). Among former drinkers, sedentary-to-sleep reallocation was associated with 2.24% lower LSM (95% CI -3.78% to -0.67%; p=0.005); among low drinkers, sedentary-to-MVPA reallocation was associated with 1.32% lower LSM (95% CI -2.19% to -0.44%; p=0.004). No substitution was significant in MetALD or ALD. The 24-hour self-reported movement behavior composition is associated with liver stiffness in MASLD, with sedentary and sleep balance showing associations in opposite directions. This supports a personalized, whole-day approach to behavioral counseling in MASLD management.

papers.title: Self-reported sleep disturbances during chemotherapy mediate circulating IL-1β effects on subjective cognitive decline in breast cancer patients.
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy can cause cognitive decline that may persist for years after treatment and reduce quality of life in cancer patients. Identifying factors during chemotherapy that contribute to post-treatment side effects could inform strategies to prevent or mitigate long-term consequences. Sleep disturbances, particularly difficulty falling or staying asleep, are highly prevalent during chemotherapy and can exacerbate cognitive symptoms. Although cross-sectional associations among cognitive decline, sleep disturbances, and inflammatory markers have been examined in cancer patients, the longitudinal dynamics of sleep and inflammation during treatment related to post-treatment cognition remain unclear. We hypothesized that increased sleep disturbances during chemotherapy predict worse cognitive decline after treatment, mediated by increased pro-inflammatory markers. To test this, 75 breast cancer patients provided blood samples to measure circulating inflammatory markers (IL-6, TNFα, IL-1β, CRP), completed questionnaires assessing sleep disturbance and perceived cognition, and underwent objective cognitive testing. Assessments occurred before, during, and approximately three months after chemotherapy. Longitudinal relationships among sleep disturbances, inflammation, and cognition were evaluated. Sleep disturbances increased during chemotherapy associated with concurrent increases in IL-6, TNFα, and IL-1β. Increased sleep disturbances during chemotherapy predicted decreased subjective, but not objective, cognition after treatment. Among inflammatory markers, increased IL-1β during chemotherapy predicted worse subjective cognition after treatment. Contrary to our hypothesis, sleep disturbances mediated the relationship between elevated IL-1β during chemotherapy and post-treatment subjective cognitive decline. These findings highlight sleep disturbance as a key, modifiable factor during chemotherapy that predicts persistent cognitive symptoms and suggest that improving sleep may mitigate cognitive deficits without directly modulating inflammation.

papers.title: Can microglia stabilize sleep and temperature under stress?
Genetic and environmental predictors of seasonality and seasonal affective disorder in individuals with depression.
papers.abstract: The etiology and nosological status of seasonal affective disorder (SAD) as a specifier of depressive episodes versus a transdiagnostic disorder are the subject of debate. In this study, we investigated the underlying etiology of SAD and dimensional seasonality by examining their association with latitude and genetic risk for a range of traits, and investigated gene-environment interactions. This study included 12,460 adults (76% female, aged 18-90) with a history of depression from the Australian Genetics of Depression Study. Regression models included predictors for latitude (distance from equator) and polygenic scores for eight traits; major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, anxiety disorders, chronotype, sleep duration, body mass index, vitamin D levels, and educational attainment. Outcomes were SAD status and general seasonality score. SAD was positively associated with latitude (OR[95%CI] = 1.05[1.03-1.06], padjusted < 0.001), and there was nominal evidence of additive and multiplicative interactions between chronotype genetic risk and latitude (OR = 0.99[0.99-0.99], padjusted = 0.381; OR = 0.98[0.97-0.99], padjusted = 0.489). General seasonality score was associated with latitude (IRR = 1.01[1.01-1.01], padjusted 0.001) and genetic risk for major depressive disorder (IRR =1.02[1.01-1.03], padjusted < 0.001), bipolar disorder (IRR = 1.02[1.01-1.03], padjusted = 0.001), anxiety disorders (IRR = 1.03[1.01-1.04], padjusted < 0.001), vitamin D levels (OR = 0.89[0.80-0.95], padjusted = 0.048), and educational attainment (IRR = 0.97[0.96-0.99], padjusted < 0.001). These findings enhance understanding of SAD etiology, highlighting contributions of psychiatric genetic risk and geographic measures on seasonal behavior, and support examining seasonality as a continuous dimension.

papers.title: Intracellular pH modulates the mechanosensitivity of OSCA/TMEM63 ion channels.
papers.abstract: Mechanosensitive (MS) channels are essential transducers that convert mechanical stimuli into biochemical signals. OSCA/TMEM63 proteins constitute a conserved family that serves as mechanical and osmotic stress sensors, yet the mechanisms by which the chemical microenvironment modulates their gating remain unclear. Here, we identify intracellular pH as a potent and side-specific regulator of OSCA/TMEM63 activity. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology, we demonstrate that OSCA/TMEM63 currents are reversibly tuned by pH: intracellular acidification suppresses channel activity, whereas alkalinization markedly potentiates it. This regulation is mediated by a pronounced shift in the mechanical activation threshold, thereby effectively tuning channel sensitivity. Our findings establish intracellular pH as a conserved modulator of OSCA/TMEM63 mechanosensitivity, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how the intracellular chemical milieu is coupled to osmo/mechano sensing.

papers.title: Subanesthetic esketamine for preventing emergence agitation after bimaxillary.
papers.abstract: Emergence agitation (EA) is common after orthognathic surgery and poses a significant threat to clinical safety. The aim of our study was to investigate the efficacy and safety of a subanesthetic dose of esketamine in preventing EA following bimaxillary orthognathic surgery. A total of 272 patients underwent bimaxillary orthognathic surgery were randomly allocated into two groups. In the esketamine group, 0.25 mg/kg esketamine was infused at the end of the surgery, whereas in the control group, placebo (normal saline) was infused. The primary endpoint was the incidence of EA (assessed with the Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale; defined as the score ≥ +2). All included patients were analyzed according to the intention-to-treat principle. The incidence of EA was significantly lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (19.1% vs 33.1%, P = 0.013). Meanwhile, patients in the esketamine group experienced a prolonged emergence time (45 [30,65]min vs 30 [20,59]min, P < 0.001) and extubation time (75 [50,119]min vs. 60 [40,99]min, P < 0.039). Moreover, subjective sleep quality on the night of surgery and postoperative anxiety and depression within the first 24 hours after surgery did not differ significantly between groups. A subanesthetic dose of esketamine administered at the end of procedure was effective in preventing EA after bimaxillary orthognathic surgery managed with a delayed extubation protocol. Given the prolonged emergence and extubation time, its use should be further evaluated for other types of surgeries that require rapid awakening and early extubation.
papers.journal: Journal of stomatology, oral and maxillofacial surgery

papers.title: A circadian clock-associated gene GmRVE8b modulates flowering time and maturity in soybean.
papers.abstract: Elucidating the regulatory mechanisms underlying flowering and maturation in soybean is essential for improving yield stability and adaptation to diverse environments. The circadian clock coordinates developmental transitions and plays a pivotal role in the regulation of reproductive development. However, the molecular mechanisms linking the circadian clock to photoperiodic and thermal responses in soybean remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a genome-wide association study using 257 diverse soybean germplasm accessions and identified GmRVE8b, a homolog of the Arabidopsis REVEILLE gene family, as a major locus significantly associated with soybean maturity across multiple environments with contrasting photoperiod regimes. Haplotype analysis showed that accessions carrying the GmRVE8bH3 haplotype matured significantly later than those harboring the GmRVE8bH1. Functional validation through transgenic overexpression further demonstrated that GmRVE8b markedly delays both flowering and maturity in soybean. Quantitative real-time PCR analysis suggested that GmRVE8b may be associated with the GmELF3-E1/E1La-FT4 photoperiodic regulatory module. Collectively, our findings suggest GmRVE8b as a previously uncharacterized circadian clock-associated negative regulator of soybean flowering and maturity, providing a promising genetic resource for molecular breeding to improve soybean adaptation across latitudes and under variable photothermal conditions.
papers.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology

papers.title: Clinical Efficacy of Inferior Turbinate Outfracture Combined with Low-Temperature Plasma Radiofrequency Ablation in Obese Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea-Hypopnea Syndrome Complicated with Nasal Obstruction.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the long-term clinical efficacy of combined inferior turbinate outfracture and low-temperature plasma radiofrequency ablation on nasal ventilation, continuous positive airway pressure tolerance, sleep status and body mass index (BMI) in obese patients with obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) complicated with bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy, whose BMI ≥28.0 kg/m2.MethodsThis single-center retrospective study enrolled a total of 40 obese OSAHS patients with bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy treated at the Department of Otorhinolaryngology, Liangxiang Hospital from August 2023 to August 2024. All subjects received combined inferior turbinate outfracture and low-temperature plasma radiofrequency ablation under general anesthesia. Outcome indicators including nasal airway resistance, apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), visual analogue scale (VAS) for nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) tolerance and BMI were detected before surgery, 1 month, 6 months and 1 year postoperatively. Polysomnography, anterior rhinomanometry and standardized scale assessment were performed uniformly at each follow-up time point. Intra-group comparisons between preoperative and postoperative data were analyzed by paired t-test; P < 0.05 was defined as statistically significant.ResultsAll 40 patients completed the 1-year standardized follow-up without loss to follow-up. Compared with preoperative baseline levels, nasal airway resistance, AHI, ESS scores and BMI were significantly decreased at 1, 6 and 12 months after surgery (all P < 0.05), while VAS scores reflecting nCPAP tolerance increased markedly (all P < 0.05). Nasal airway resistance remained stable at a low level within one year after operation. AHI and BMI were further reduced at postoperative 1 year compared with 1 month after surgery (P < 0.05), and ESS scores achieved the optimal improvement at postoperative 6 months.ConclusionObservations from this case series suggest that the combined inferior turbinate outfracture and low-temperature plasma radiofrequency ablation may represent a feasible minimally invasive surgical option for obese OSAHS patients with nasal obstruction, inferior turbinate hypertrophy and documented CPAP intolerance. Within this cohort, we observed postoperative reductions in nasal airway resistance, AHI, ESS scores and BMI, accompanied by improved self-reported nCPAP tolerance. However, we cannot quantify how much of these improvements stem from nasal surgery versus weight loss, CPAP use or other unmeasured factors. A reduction in BMI cannot be interpreted as evidence that surgery induces weight loss. The hypothesis of a positive therapeutic cycle remains speculative, as data regarding diet, exercise, weight-loss interventions and objective CPAP usage were not collected. No postoperative infection or active bleeding was observed in the present cohort; nevertheless, other potential complications were not systematically assessed, so the safety profile of this procedure cannot be fully determined. This surgical approach avoids the high perioperative risks of traditional extensive pharyngeal surgery and provides a potential observational reference for obese OSAHS patients with severe nasal stenosis.

papers.title: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery for Treatment of Obesity and Related Diseases.
papers.abstract: Metabolic surgery has emerged as the most effective long-term treatment for obesity, a global health epidemic associated with serious conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea. Updated 2022 guidelines have expanded eligibility, allowing more patients to benefit from surgical intervention. Modern procedures-including sleeve gastrectomy, SADI-S, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and duodenal switch-are now safer, with low morbidity and mortality rates. Careful preoperative planning, multidisciplinary evaluation, and proper procedure selection are essential for optimal outcomes. Advances in laparoscopic and robotic techniques, along with adherence to sound surgical principles, help minimize complications and improve patient safety and long-term success.
papers.journal: The Surgical clinics of North America

papers.title: Environment-specific virtual head direction representation in the human anteroventral thalamus during memory-guided spatial orientation.
papers.abstract: Knowing which way you are facing is essential for navigation. In animals, a dedicated set of neurons-head direction cells-acts as an internal compass: each cell fires most strongly when the animal faces a particular direction. The anterior thalamus is a key hub for this system. In humans, however, direct electrophysiological evidence for a comparable head direction signal remains limited. To address this gap, we recorded intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) from the anteroventral thalamus (AVT) in patients with epilepsy while they performed a virtual navigation task. We analyzed neural activity during in-place rotation to isolate virtual head direction (vHD) information. Using inverted encoding models applied to multi-band neural activity, we reconstructed continuous vHD within two distinct virtual environments. Critically, the decoders failed to generalize across environments, indicating that the AVT vHD representation is environment specific rather than a fixed, universal map. This encoding was observed in the AVT and was temporally specific to rotation epochs; no significant encoding was detected in the pulvinar, another thalamic subregion not part of the classic head direction network in rodents. Together, these findings suggest that the human AVT carries environment-specific vHD information, bridging a gap between animal models and human navigation and highlighting a potential link to spatial disorientation disorders.

papers.title: Circadian syndrome as a multisystem risk factor for pain in older adults: Evidence from a cross-sectional and longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Circadian syndrome and pain are prevalent in aging populations, yet their relationship remains underexplored. This study investigates the cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between circadian syndrome and pain among older adults. Data were drawn from three prospective cohorts: the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, the English Longitudinal Study of Aging, and the US Health and Retirement Study. Pain severity was self-reported as mild, moderate, or severe. Multivariable logistic regression assessed cross-sectional associations, while generalized linear mixed models examined longitudinal relationships between baseline circadian syndrome and incident pain during follow-up. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were conducted to confirm the reliability of the findings. At baseline, 18,719 participants were included, comprising 7219 from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, 6063 from the English Longitudinal Study of Aging, and 5437 from the Health and Retirement Study. Cross-sectionally, individuals with circadian syndrome had significantly higher odds of prevalent pain than those without: the odds ratios were 1.68 (95% confidence interval 1.51-1.88) in the Chinese cohort, 2.24 (95% confidence interval 1.95-2.58) in the English cohort, and 1.71 (95% confidence interval 1.52-1.93) in the US cohort, suggesting a positive association between circadian syndrome and prevalent pain. In longitudinal analyses, baseline circadian syndrome predicted an increased risk of new-onset pain, with odds ratios of 1.26 (95% confidence interval 1.11-1.44) in the Chinese cohort, 1.62 (95% confidence interval 1.26-2.09) in the English cohort, and 1.22 (95% confidence interval 1.05-1.42) in the US cohort, providing stronger evidence for prospective prediction. Results remained robust across subgroup and sensitivity analyses. This large-scale multinational study establishes circadian syndrome as a significant correlate of both prevalent and incident pain in older adults, highlighting the importance of multisystem circadian health in pain risk assessment.

papers.title: Resting EEG as a condition-dependent ageing phenotype.
papers.abstract: Resting-state electroencephalography is increasingly proposed as a scalable marker of healthy brain ageing, yet its interpretability depends on distinguishing stable individual characteristics from condition-dependent measurement effects. This secondary analysis of an open lifespan dataset examined periodic alpha activity, alpha-peak detectability, aperiodic spectral structure, short-term repeatability, and longitudinal change under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions before and after an extended cognitive battery. Eye state strongly organised both whether a posterior alpha peak could be detected and the values of periodic and aperiodic measures. Age-related trajectories were prominent for the aperiodic exponent and full-sample alpha activity, whereas evidence that age modified post-battery change was weak. Across follow-up, detectable alpha frequency and the aperiodic exponent showed mean decreases, while alpha power was comparatively stable. Level measures demonstrated moderate-to-high repeatability and rank-order stability, but post-battery and difference-in-differences change scores were considerably less reliable. The findings position resting EEG as a condition-dependent ageing phenotype rather than a unitary baseline. They further show that peak detection, recording context, attrition, and the reliability of change must be modelled explicitly when resting EEG is used for lifespan inference or normative applications.

papers.title: From one risky choice to the next: Trait dominance, feedback, and response-locked EEG in corporate leaders.
papers.abstract: Repeated risky choice can reflect both the direction of choice and whether a previous choice is repeated, but these patterns are not always distinguished in research on trait dominance. In this secondary analysis, 28 male corporate leaders completed a repeated monetary gambling task with complete feedback while EEG was recorded. Mixed-effects models examined associations of trait dominance, choice history, and feedback with subsequent High-risk choice, Stay/Switch behavior, response time, and response-locked FCz activity. Higher dominance was associated with greater odds of choosing High after both previous High- and Low-risk choices, with no reliable difference between the two history-specific associations. In the direct transition model, a 1-SD increase in continuous dominance corresponded to 47% higher odds of Current High choice (OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.25, 1.73]). On the Stay/Switch scale, higher dominance predicted staying after High but switching after Low, indicating a High-directed pattern rather than uniformly greater repetition of the preceding risk level. Recent outcomes also remained consequential: absolute valence and comparative favorability were associated with subsequent choice, and responses were 12.7% slower after Gains than Losses, whereas dominance was not reliably related to response time. EEG findings were more qualified: mean FCz voltage was more positive in the predefined High-dominance group, whereas peak latency showed a feedback-dependent dominance contrast between Gain-Correct and Gain-Error trials; no individual condition-specific dominance slope survived Holm correction. Trait dominance was therefore associated most clearly with the direction of repeated risky choice, while recent experience continued to shape the next decision.

papers.title: Eye movement and EEG features in generalized anxiety disorder.
papers.abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is a common psychiatric condition that severely impacts individuals' mental health and quality of life. However, its diagnosis and treatment remain challenging in clinical practice, largely relying on subjective assessments and lacking objective, quantitative biological markers. Therefore, this study aimed to compare eye movement and electroencephalography (EEG) features between GAD patients and healthy controls, and to evaluate the classification performance of eye movement, EEG, and their combined features using machine learning. Twenty-nine GAD patients and 27 healthy controls were recruited. Clinical symptoms, cognitive function, eye movement, and EEG data were collected. Descriptive statistics and partial correlation analyses were conducted to compare group differences and explore feature associations. A linear support vector machine (SVM) model was constructed using eye movement, EEG, and combined features for classification. GAD patients exhibited eye movement abnormalities, including reduced fixation duration, increased saccade velocity, enlarged vertical saccade amplitude, and prolonged antisaccade latency, as well as abnormal beta power during Go/Nogo tasks. The model combining eye movement and EEG features achieved the best overall performance, outperforming models based on eye movement or EEG features alone. The relatively small sample size warrants further validation in larger cohorts. Multimodal neurophysiological features integrating eye movement and EEG improve classification performance for GAD and may serve as potential objective biomarkers.

papers.title: Respiratory burden and periodic limb movement frequency in adults with elevated PLMI: A retrospective polysomnographic study.
papers.abstract: Periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS) frequently coexist with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and whether PLMS should be scored when OSA is untreated remains unclear. In adults with an elevated periodic limb movement index (PLMI), we primarily examined whether the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) was associated with PLMI; secondary analyses assessed its associations with the PLM-arousal index (PLMAI) and PLM-arousal coupling. We retrospectively analyzed polysomnograms of 507 consecutive adults with PLMI ≥15 events/h. Associations of respiratory and oxygenation measures with PLMI were assessed using Spearman correlation, adjusted regression of log-transformed PLMI, and categorical analyses across OSA severity. PLMAI was modeled using mean-centered PLMI and AHI, their interaction, age, sex, and body mass index, with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) inference and sensitivity analyses. AHI was not associated with PLMI (ρ = 0.003; 95% CI -0.08 to 0.09). After adjustment for age, sex, and body mass index, PLMI changed by -0.2% per 10 events/h of AHI (95% CI -2.2% to 1.8%). PLMI did not differ across OSA severity categories (p = 0.63), and AHI did not predict PLMI >30 events/h (OR per 10 events/h 1.05; 95% CI 0.98-1.12). AHI showed no independent main association with PLMAI (p = 0.08), but the PLMI×AHI interaction was positive and remained significant across sensitivity analyses (HC3 p < 0.001). In adults with elevated PLMI, respiratory burden was not associated with PLM frequency, supporting continued scoring and reporting of PLMS in patients with OSA. Higher AHI modestly strengthened the association between PLMI and PLM-related arousals; therefore, PLMAI should be interpreted cautiously when the respiratory burden is substantial.

papers.title: REFS: Robust EEG feature selection with incomplete labels for multi-dimensional emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Compared to single-type features, multi-type electroencephalography (EEG) features provide a multi-level representation for analyzing multi-dimensional emotions. However, the high dimensionality of multi-type EEG features, combined with the relatively small number of high-quality EEG samples, poses challenges such as classifier overfitting and suboptimal real-time performance in the multi-dimensional emotion recognition task. As the number of EEG channels increases, the issue will become increasingly severe. Moreover, practical applications of affective brain-computer interface frequently encounters partial absence of multi-dimensional emotional label data due to diverse emotional self-assessment models, and ambiguity and variability in individual emotion perception. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel robust EEG feature selection method for incomplete multi-dimensional emotion recognition. The method leverages adaptive orthogonal latent semantic indexing to reconstruct the multi-dimensional emotional label space through second-order and higher-order relations, which could reduce the negative impact of missing values and outliers on label reconstruction. Simultaneously, it employs least squares regression with graph-based manifold learning regularization and global feature redundancy minimization regularization to enable EEG feature subset selection despite missing information, ultimately achieving robust and fast EEG-based multi-dimensional emotion recognition. The proposed method was validated on three multi-dimensional emotional datasets with varying channel configurations, namely DREAMER, DEAP and HDED, under different label missing ratios. Experimental results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms thirteen state-of-the-art feature selection methods in terms of robustness for EEG emotional feature selection across various missing ratios. The proposed method provides a robust and efficient solution for feature selection in multi-dimensional emotion recognition under incomplete EEG label scenarios, delivering reliable performance for practical affective brain-computer interface applications.

papers.title: Open-Source, High-Speed and High-Resolution Data Acquisition Platform for Biopotential Recordings and Neural EIT applications.
papers.abstract: Biopotential measurement devices, such as EEG, ECG, and EMG recorders, are available in low-cost, open-source implementations with standard specifications. However, high-end systems remain expensive and predominantly proprietary, limiting accessibility and customization by research laboratories. In addition, neurophysiology techniques such as bioimpedance-based Fast Neural Electrical Impedance Tomography (FN-EIT) also rely on these systems for data acquisition. This work aimed to develop an open-source biopotential recording system using off-the-shelf components that achieves performance comparable to high-end devices. We designed our system to provide simultaneous sampling over 32 channels, 24-bit resolution, 10 kHz bandwidth, 50 kHz sampling rate, and battery-powered operation while reducing cost by two orders of magnitude. System performance was evaluated comparatively against a reference device. Initial validation involved benchtop recordings in saline solution and standard non-invasive biopotential measurements (ECG and EMG). Further in-vivo validation was performed by recording evoked electrophysiological responses and FN-EIT traces from the sciatic nerve of a rat during tibial branch stimulation. EMG recordings showed comparable RMS peak amplitudes (814±153 µV vs. 897±113µV, p=0.07), while ECG-derived heart rates closely matched between systems (64.8±4.0 bpm vs. 65.1±3.1bpm, p=0.54). During in-vivo recordings, compound action potentials exhibited comparable amplitudes and morphology (129±26 mV vs 128±25 mV, P=0.15). FN-EIT recordings showed strongly correlated baseline voltages (R>0.93, P=0.11), sub-microvolt noise levels (0.83±0.36µV vs. 0.42±0.25µV, p<0.05), and comparable impedance variations (0.006±0.002% vs 0.005±0.003, P>0.05). FN-EIT images of functional activity recorded with the novel device closely matched reference ones, exhibiting a 98.5% overlap in activated area. The proposed open-source device has the potential to broaden research access to customizable, high-specification data acquisition hardware and facilitate wider adoption of specialized neural recording techniques such as FN-EIT.

papers.title: Accurate EEG-based linear state-space model of cortical dynamics during a passive motor task with exogenous input.
papers.abstract: Revealing the dynamics of the brain in the presence of exogenous inputs iscrucial for mechanistic understanding, interventions and regulations. We study state-spacemathematical modeling of brain's cortical dynamics using electroencephalography (EEG)data in an experiment with continuous exogenous input. We use subspaceidentification techniques to model the brain dynamics in a passive motor task experiment.The EEG data were recorded while participants were seated with their wrist strapped to ahaptic manipulator. The manipulator imposed a continuous multisine angularperturbation to the wrist as the exogenous input to the brain. Using twosubspace identification algorithms, we show that linear time-invariant state-space modelsaccurately represent the measurements, in a latent space, assuming that the EEG data arethe models' output. The model is verified and validated using data from sevenparticipants. Moreover, we construct linear maps to relate the latent space dynamics tothe neural source space. We verify that the findings of our model align with thoseidentified in previous studies. Accurate linear model in the presence ofexogenous input provides a pathway for designing parsimonious and simple controllers. Inaddition, it enables development of online monitoring, connectivity analysis and controlrelevant to neurorehabilitation, motor learning, and brain-computer interfacing.

papers.title: Migraine burden and occupational impact among corporate employees attending neurology clinics in Skardu, Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan.
papers.abstract: Objectives. Migraine is a leading cause of disability worldwide, yet remains underdiagnosed in low and middle-income countries. This study assessed the clinical features, triggers, management patterns and occupational impact of neurologist-diagnosed migraine among corporate employees in Skardu, Pakistan. Methods. A cross-sectional study of adult corporate employees with neurologist-confirmed migraine was conducted at neurology outpatient clinics in Skardu, Gilgit-Baltistan. Data were collected via a validated questionnaire on demographics, clinical features, triggers, occupational impact and management. Non-parametric tests and multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of high occupational impact, reported as adjusted odds ratios and p values. Results. Most participants were female (72.4%) and aged 26-35 years (43.0%), with migraine without aura being the most common (40.6%). The mean migraine burden was high (58.9 ± 13.6) and varied significantly by gender, age and management. Poor management (34.7%) and reliance on Over-the-Counter (OTC) analgesics (65.3%) were common. Work impact was substantial, with 44% reporting moderate-to-severe absenteeism and 55% presenteeism. High occupational impact was independently predicted by higher migraine burden, frequent attacks (>6/month), stress, sleep deprivation, environmental stressors, poor management and information technology-sector employment. Conclusion. Among corporate employees in Skardu, migraine causes significant absenteeism and workplace impairment; addressing triggers and improving specialist care can reduce disability.
papers.journal: International journal of occupational safety and ergonomics : JOSE

papers.title: The influence of overwork on residents' depression risk during the COVID-19 pandemic in China.
papers.abstract: Combined with China Family Panel Studies data in 2020 completed during the COVID-19 pandemic, this article examined the impact of overwork on residents' depression risk and its mechanism. The results show that overwork will significantly increase residents' depression risk, and this result is valid after endogenous and robust tests. Heterogeneity analysis shows that overwork has a stronger positive impact on depression risk among young people, rural residents and highly educated talents. Quantile regression reveals that as the quantile of the depression level increases, overwork exacerbates the likelihood of residents facing higher depression risk. The moderation analysis indicates that Internet use intensifies the positive impact of overwork on residents' depression risk, while an increase in social status weakens the positive impact of overwork on residents' depression risk. The mediation analysis showed that overwork exacerbates residents' depression risk by reducing exercise frequency, lowering sleep quality and decreasing family interaction.
papers.journal: International journal of occupational safety and ergonomics : JOSE

papers.title: Epithelial function of the circadian clock gene, Bmal1, in regulating the mucosa.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms, 24-hour repeating oscillations in daily physiology, are implicated in maintaining intestinal homeostasis. These rhythms are driven by the circadian clock, a molecular timekeeper found throughout cells of the body, including those of the intestinal epithelium. Loss of clock function has been found to worsen colitis; however, it is not clear how the clock impacts regeneration which enables a tissue to return to its homeostatic set point following an injury. To investigate these questions, we used a conditional knockout of the core clock gene, Bmal1, in mouse colon epithelial cells. Our data show that prior to injury Bmal1 promotes colon mucus production, which increases in thickness and abundance within goblet cells when mice are active and begin feeding. Bmal1 loss lowers mucus production but does not drive an apparent tissue phenotype until the system is injured and regenerates itself. In this context, Bmal1 epithelial loss drives a male-specific colitis exacerbation and a delay in the ability of colon epithelial cells of both male and female mice to resolve injury to return to their homeostatic set point. Our data suggest that epithelial sex-specific clock rhythms are needed for optimal colon barrier homeostasis.

papers.title: TMEM175: Lysosomal Ion Channel Physiology, Therapeutic Potential, and Emerging Pharmacology.
papers.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175) is a lysosomal cation channel that has emerged as a promising drug target for Parkinson's disease (PD). Genetic and functional studies linking TMEM175 loss-of-function variants to increased PD risk, lysosomal dysfunction, and α-synuclein accumulation have generated considerable interest in developing pharmacological approaches to enhance channel activity. As a lysosomal cation channel with reported K+ and H+ permeability, TMEM175 regulates lysosomal membrane potential, pH stability, autophagic flux, and degradative capacity, placing it at a critical control point for cellular proteostasis. Recent advances in high-throughput screening, automated and lysosomal patch clamp electrophysiology, cryoelectron microscopy, and structure-guided medicinal chemistry have transformed TMEM175 from a relatively obscure lysosomal ion channel into a tractable drug target. These approaches have enabled the discovery of multiple classes of TMEM175 modulators while providing new insights into channel gating and mechanisms of activation. In this review, we summarize current progress in TMEM175 pharmacology, including advances in functional assay development and the emerging landscape of tool compounds used to study channel function. We discuss TMEM175 physiology and structure-function relationships, the growing evidence supporting therapeutic intervention, and recent discoveries revealing multiple mechanisms of channel activation. Finally, we highlight key challenges that remain for the field, including the development of potent and selective modulators, opportunities afforded by synergistic channel activation, and the potential application of TMEM175-directed therapeutics beyond Parkinson's disease in a broader range of neurodegenerative and lysosome-associated disorders.

papers.title: Beyond Estrogen: Aging and Declining Cardiac Autonomic Modulation Are Linked to Longer QTc After Menopause.
papers.abstract: Women are more susceptible than men to QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias, yet how aging and cardiac autonomic control jointly affect the QTc interval in women, independent of fluctuating sex hormones, remains unclear. We hypothesized that QTc is longer in postmenopausal than in young women, and that this difference reflects aging and age-related changes in cardiac autonomic control rather than sex-hormone levels. We studied 64 healthy menstruating women (median age 29.5 years) in the early follicular phase, when estrogen and progesterone are low, and 35 healthy postmenopausal women (median age 67 years). This design minimized acute hormonal differences. QT intervals and heart rate variability (HRV; power spectral analysis) were measured. QT, QTc and JTc, the latter reflecting ventricular repolarization, were longer in postmenopausal women (P < 0.001; η2 ≥ 0.14). Postmenopausal women also had lower ln-transformed total power (P < 0.001), LF power (P = 0.006; η² = 0.09) and HF power (P < 0.001; η2 = 0.17), and a higher LF/HF ratio (P < 0.001; η2 = 0.16). In postmenopausal women, QTc correlated modestly and negatively with total power and LF power (both P = 0.02), but not in young women. Because acute hormonal differences were minimized, the longer QTc after menopause is more consistent with aging and reduced cardiac autonomic modulation than with the prevailing sex-hormone milieu. These findings suggest that age-related autonomic decline, together with a higher LF/HF ratio, may contribute to QT vulnerability in postmenopausal women, with implications for arrhythmic risk assessment and QT-prolonging drug prescription.
papers.journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology

papers.title: Orexin Deficiency and Cardiometabolic Risk in Narcolepsy: Mechanistic Pathways and Therapeutic Implications.
papers.abstract: Narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) results from autoimmune destruction of orexin-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. While traditionally viewed as a sleep disorder, accumulating evidence indicates that orexin deficiency produces widespread cardiometabolic consequences - including obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, metabolic associated steatotic liver disease, and major adverse cardiovascular events - that cannot be fully explained by weight gain or medication effects alone. This review examines four overlapping mechanisms through which orexin deficiency drives cardiometabolic risk. First, loss of orexin disrupts the coupling of hunger drive with arousal and energy expenditure. Orexin neurons interact with NPY/AgRP and POMC circuits and project to reward and cognitive control pathways; their absence impairs satiety signaling, blunts hedonic reward processing, and uncouples food intake from physical activity. Second, orexin has direct peripheral metabolic effects - enhancing beta-cell function, promoting adipocyte insulin sensitivity, and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis. Loss of these actions promotes insulin resistance, atherogenic dyslipidemia, and hepatic steatosis. Third, disrupted sleep architecture and autonomic dysfunction compound metabolic risk. Orexin loss produces state-dependent dysautonomia - reduced resting sympathetic drive with inadequate parasympathetic compensation during sleep - contributing to non-dipping blood pressure and elevated cardiovascular risk. Disease-specific barriers including cataplexy avoidance further limit physical activity. Fourth, the autoimmune inflammatory process may contribute to systemic metabolic inflammation, though the extent of ongoing inflammation after neuronal loss remains uncertain. These mechanisms are interdependent and mutually reinforcing. Selective orexin receptor 2 agonists such as oveporexton offer the first opportunity to restore lost orexin signaling. Whether this translates into cardiometabolic improvements warrants systematic evaluation in future trials.

papers.title: Effects of 24-h sleep deprivation on circulating irisin, BDNF, and soluble klotho responses during exercise in the heat in young and older males.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation and heat stress commonly coexist in occupational, athletic, and environmental settings and may disproportionately increase physiological strain in older adults. We examined whether 24-h sleep deprivation alters circulating biomarkers linked to proposed roles in metabolic adaptation (irisin), neurophysiological regulation (BDNF), and cellular stress protection (soluble klotho) during exercise in the heat in young and older males. Ten young (23±3 years) and ten older (61±4 years) males completed randomized crossover trials involving normal sleep and 24-h total sleep deprivation before three 30-min bouts of semi-recumbent cycling in hot, dry conditions (40°C, ∼13% relative humidity). Blood samples were obtained before and at end-exercise for measurement of irisin, BDNF, and soluble klotho (s-klotho). Older males exhibited lower circulating concentrations of all three biomarkers across conditions and time points than young males. Exercise in the heat increased irisin (mean change 522.7 pg/mL, 95% CI 310.6 to 734.8, p<0.001, q<0.001), whereas no statistically significant overall pre-to-end change was observed for BDNF or s-klotho. The irisin response appeared smaller in older than young males when averaged across sleep conditions (between-group difference 458.1 pg/mL, 95% CI 34.0 to 882.3, p=0.035) but did not remain significant after correction across the three age × time contrasts (q=0.104) and is therefore hypothesis-generating. However, the study did not detect evidence that 24-h sleep deprivation altered circulating irisin, BDNF, or s-klotho responses in either age group. These findings demonstrate age-related differences in circulating biomarker concentrations, but do not establish corresponding differences in physiological adaptability or biomarker responsiveness.

papers.title: Sleep Variables in Health Research: From Systematic Omission to Methodological Integration - A Narrative Review and Proposal.
papers.abstract: For decades, sample characterization in health and physiological research has relied on a "triad of convenience": demographics, anthropometrics, and socioeconomic status. While these parameters offer a baseline description, they systematically omit a critical biological variable sustaining human homeostasis: sleep. This baseline omission introduces significant residual confounding, creating a "Table 1 Fallacy" where matched cohorts appear identical but remain physiologically heterogeneous due to unmeasured sleep-wake variance, including duration, quality, and circadian alignment. Sleep occupies a unique position among neglected baseline variables because it simultaneously coordinates neuroendocrine secretion, immune priming, autonomic regulation, and metabolic clearance within each circadian cycle, mechanistic roles that differentiate it from other lifestyle factors currently absent from reporting guidelines. Compelling evidence demonstrates that sleep duration, quality, and chronotype directly modulate peripheral insulin sensitivity, hormonal balance, immune readiness, and cardiovascular function. Failing to account for these metrics can lead to the misclassification of participants as "non-responders" in clinical trials, masking true primary intervention effects or creating an illusion of treatment efficacy. To restore reproducibility and scientific rigor, we contend that sleep reporting must transition from a voluntary act to a methodological mandate in studies where sleep represents a biologically plausible source of confounding. We propose a high-yield, low-cost Minimal Sleep Set (MSS) utilizing validated screening tools to systematically control for sleep-wake variance, ensuring that the human biological state is as clearly defined as the intervention itself.
authors: Adryel Luciano de Souza Matoso Alves

papers.title: Toolkits to Support Health Care Providers in Health Behavior Change for Patients With Chronic Conditions: Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Health care providers (HCPs) are key agents in supporting health behavior (eg, smoking and physical activity) change in patients. Toolkits have previously been used to guide HCPs in care and have shown effectiveness in improving clinical outcomes. However, there is a lack of understanding of how toolkits should be developed to best support HCPs. This scoping review aimed to map the existing literature on the theories, models, frameworks, approaches, and methods that have been used in the development of toolkits to support HCPs in health behavior change. Five databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Scopus) were searched from inception to August 2026. Original research articles published in peer-reviewed academic journals in English from any geographic area describing the development of a toolkit to support HCPs in health behavior change for patients with chronic conditions were included. Qualitative data were analyzed using conventional content analysis and quantitative data were examined in tabular terms, with a simple descriptive synthesis of the findings. Barriers and facilitators identified from studies were deductively coded using the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) and reported according to TDF domains identified in studies. Nineteen articles met inclusion criteria. The articles included toolkits addressing several health behaviors, including physical activity (n=16), nutrition (n=6), sedentary behavior (n=2), sleep (n=2), and weight management more broadly (n=2). Toolkit formats (eg, use of videos and written components) varied greatly between studies. All studies included knowledge users in the development of the toolkit. Use of a theory, model, or framework was described in 14 studies, and barriers and facilitators to HCP promotion of health behavior change were examined in 14 studies. The most frequently reported TDF domain was environmental context and resources, with time as the most frequently cited barrier. Toolkit development typically consisted of an exploratory phase to determine knowledge users' needs and wants, toolkit development, dissemination, and evaluation. Toolkits varied greatly in format and development process but generally involved iterative development based on feedback from knowledge users. However, no toolkits targeted smoking, alcohol use, or recreational drug use, which warrant further study. To assist future investigators looking to develop a toolkit for health behavior change, we present a definition of a toolkit and a series of recommendations for toolkit design and development. Although previous reviews have mapped the existence of various toolkits, they have not examined how these have been developed. This review provides a novel description of this development and a guide for the development of future toolkits to increase uptake of toolkits and reduce the knowledge-to-practice gap. Additionally, this review defines the term "toolkit" and identifies its minimum components, which can be used by researchers to classify and compare toolkits in the future.
